ns.prompt: Eight systems, one 15-hour night shift. Pick your specialty and rack two tools — every system shows its price before you touch it, and every miss becomes a live incident you must contain.
ns.legend[0].label: Criticality 1 — desk systems
ns.legend[1].label: Criticality 2 — production
ns.legend[2].label: Criticality 3 — crown jewels

ns-0001.why: The GDPR right to data portability entitles a person to the data they provided in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable form, normally within one month. A self-service export makes that the default. A contract cannot waive a statutory right, PDFs still fail the format test however carefully reviewed, and deletion is a different right (erasure) that she never invoked.

ns-0002.why: The stick itself is real evidence: a physical object presented in its own right, so its value depends on identification and an unbroken chain of custody from seizure onward. Imaging supports analysis but never replaces the original, and discarding it loses the best evidence. Returning items or leaving them with the finder breaks custody and invites an authenticity challenge.

ns-0003.why: Access removal must coincide with termination; a dismissed insider with a live session on the settlement cluster is an active threat. Cut the session and disable the accounts, keeping the logs, then inform HR. Waiting or watching lets harm happen for the sake of a nicer record, and a password reset does not end a session that is already authenticated.

ns-0004.why: Contain first: pull the message and kill the stolen credentials, then give staff a short, just-in-time alert with a clear reporting path so they become sensors for the rest of the wave. A course is education on a slow cadence and will not stop tonight's clicks. Punishing the clickers teaches people to hide mistakes, which kills the reporting you need.

ns-0005.why: A risk acceptance holds only for the conditions that were assessed. A public exploit and active scanning change the likelihood, so the risk owner must decide again, while an interim control keeps exposure inside tolerance. Hiding behind the old signature ignores changed risk, decommissioning on your own authority oversteps the owner, and an unsupported product transfers nothing to its vendor.

ns-0006.why: A guideline is a recommended, non-mandatory practice: it informs judgement and yields to the incident response procedure and emergency change path when a key is being abused. Treating advice as a hard rule leaves the key live for days. Exception requests exist for departing from mandatory policy, not advice, and rewriting documents mid-incident does nothing to stop the attacker.

ns-0007.why: The business impact analysis already set maximum tolerable downtimes and recovery priorities; the settlement batch, with payment cut-offs behind it, likely has the tightest one. Follow the plan rather than the noise. Loud complaints are not criticality, runbooks should be reachable offline rather than drive the order, and an equal split slows the most critical recovery.

ns-0008.why: A technical (logical) control acts inside the system itself, so a DLP block and account suspension stop the exfiltration within minutes. The alternatives are the wrong type for a live leak: reminders and contract clauses are administrative controls that deter slowly, and a guard is a physical control that cannot stop a network upload in progress.

ns-0009.why: This is a software supply chain compromise: a valid signature proves where the code came from, not that it is safe. Contain the affected hosts and stop further pushes through the abused channel, then work the supplier's incident obligations. Switching vendors overnight swaps one unassessed supplier for another, waiting trusts the compromised channel, and withholding payment contains nothing.

ns-0010.why: Trading enterprise revenue against risk is a governance decision reserved for the executive committee; the incident plan's escalation path should name the executive who holds it on call. Security informs the decision with the containment options and impact. Shutting the service yourself exceeds delegated authority, a team lead has no enterprise mandate, and waiting for the board leaves the intruder active.

ns-0011.why: Threat modelling identifies and ranks threats and specifies mitigations, but nothing is protected until those security controls are deployed in production. The analysis is done; the gap is implementation, so an emergency change closes it now. Re-running or expanding the model is analysis while data leaks, and a next-sprint fix accepts ongoing harm nobody has approved.

ns-0012.why: Hacking back is unauthorised access: illegal, and against the ISC2 Code's canon to act honourably, justly, responsibly and legally. The server may belong to an innocent, compromised owner. Defend your own perimeter and report to parties with authority. Logging in 'just for evidence' is still unauthorised access, and doing it off the corporate network adds deceit to the offence.

ns-0013.why: Publicly traded companies in the US must disclose material cybersecurity incidents: SEC rules require a Form 8-K within four business days of deciding an incident is material, and executives answer for accurate reporting. Route it to the disclosure committee and legal. Sitting on it risks securities liability, an unreviewed website post pre-empts that process, and tipping selected merchants is selective disclosure.

ns-0014.why: A criminal court needs proof beyond reasonable doubt, built on evidence that survives admissibility challenges. Contain the access, collect forensically sound images under chain of custody, and involve law enforcement, who carry the prosecution. Browsing the live machine alters the evidence, a remote wipe destroys it, and warning the suspect invites evidence destruction and flight.

ns-0015.why: This is mandatory vacation doing its job: fraud that needs constant tending surfaces when someone else runs the process. Now remove her access, preserve the records and let HR and legal investigate. Calling her first tips off a suspect who is logged in right now; reversing refunds disturbs the trail; recalling her from leave hands the process straight back to the person under suspicion.

ns-0016.why: This is vishing: social engineering by voice, using authority and urgency. Identity must be verified through an independently sourced channel, such as calling back the number on file, never with details a caller can research. Reverse the completed reset and review that account, then brief the desk. Employee numbers leak easily, and bowing to rank is exactly what the attacker is exploiting.

ns-0017.why: Senior management holds ultimate responsibility for risk decisions; security advises, it does not own business risk. An acceptance must be signed by someone with authority over the business consequence, with the exposure and interim controls spelled out. A text message is not a formal delegation, an analyst has no authority to accept, and acting unilaterally sidesteps the owner entirely.

ns-0018.why: A procedure is the mandatory step-by-step instruction that makes results repeatable and evidence-safe, which is exactly what the runbook section is for. Improvised methods destroy volatile memory and make the containment record inconsistent. Waiting for a policy rewrite confuses the policy, which says what must happen, with the procedure, which says how.

ns-0019.why: Business continuity planning starts with senior management: they sponsor it, commit resources, approve scope and ultimately own the plan, and a cross-functional team does the work. Continuity covers business processes, not just IT, so an IT-authored, self-approved plan lacks both breadth and authority. Software does not create commitment, and backups are a recovery detail, not the plan.

ns-0020.why: An ordinary user reaching an admin function is STRIDE's elevation of privilege, and the mitigation is authorisation enforced on the server for every call. Hiding the button is security through obscurity; anyone can call the endpoint directly. The caller is already authenticated, so password rules miss the flaw, and rate limiting only slows the abuse down.

ns-0021.why: Safeguard value is ALE before minus ALE after minus the control's annual cost: 20,000 − 4,000 − 90,000 leaves minus €74,000. A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is not cost-justified, so look for cheaper mitigation or have the owner accept the risk. Effectiveness alone is not a business case, and brand harm should be estimated, not assumed.

ns-0022.why: This is an administrative investigation: an internal policy matter whose outcome is HR action, so a lower standard of proof applies and the scope stays proportionate to the acceptable use policy. Evidence is still gathered and documented properly. The police handle crimes, a shift-floor confrontation compromises the inquiry, and covert keylogging is disproportionate and may breach privacy law.

ns-0023.why: The property that failed is integrity, along with proof of origin. A digital signature verified on arrival detects any alteration and binds the sheet to the carrier that sent it. Encryption at rest protects confidentiality after the sheet has arrived, a second server serves availability, and read restrictions are confidentiality again. Match the control to the property that broke.

ns-0024.why: Pre-employment screening scaled to the role's sensitivity, such as references, identity, and criminal and credit checks for someone approving payouts, must be complete before access is granted; afterwards is too late. An NDA is a different control with a different purpose. Screening by nationality is discriminatory and says nothing about the risk the role carries.

ns-0025.why: An RTO comes out of the business impact analysis: impact over time gives the maximum tolerable downtime, and the RTO must sit inside it. Only the process owners know the fines, delays and contract penalties involved. An industry default ignores Tessaly's impacts, IT's current capability is an input to strategy rather than the requirement, and a zero RTO is rarely cost-justified.

ns-0026.why: Good governance needs independence: a security function reporting to the executive it must sometimes challenge creates a conflict of interest, and direct board access supports oversight. Shared budgets do not remove the conflict, and self-certification by the conflicted executive is weak assurance. Spreading the role across engineers removes the single point of accountability that governance depends on.

ns-0027.why: An awareness programme is judged by the behaviour it changes, not the activity it logs. Report and click rates show whether people act differently, and the gaps they reveal tell you which content to rework. Completion is a vanity metric, a longer course adds seat time rather than skill, and a harder quiz changes the dashboard without changing anyone's behaviour.

ns-0028.why: Standards turn policy intent into specific, mandatory requirements, here a configuration baseline every scanner must meet, which also gives auditors something to test against. Restating the policy adds nothing enforceable. An optional guideline recreates the inconsistency that is failing audits, and a reminder email is not a control at all.

ns-0029.why: GDPR restricts transfers of personal data outside the EEA. Without an adequacy decision you need an approved mechanism such as standard contractual clauses, backed by a transfer impact assessment. Encryption helps but is not a legal basis, the provider obeying local law may itself be the risk, and silence is never valid consent, which employees can rarely give freely anyway.

ns-0030.why: The ISC2 Code asks you to act honourably and honestly, and an undisclosed conflict of interest undermines both, however fair your scoring. Disclosure lets the organisation manage it. Genuine merit does not cure the appearance of bias, marking the bid down is dishonest in the other direction, and a silent exit hides the conflict instead of surfacing it.

ns-0031.why: Supply chain risk includes delivery: hardware can be tampered with in transit, and an unexpected courier plus resealed boxes means custody cannot be trusted. Verify serial numbers, seals and firmware with the supplier before anything touches card data. An approved catalogue says nothing about this shipment, a scan will not find a hardware skimmer, and cancelling the contract acts before the facts are known.

ns-0032.why: Rare, high-impact residual risk is the classic case for transfer: purchasing cybersecurity insurance shifts the financial impact, although accountability for the risk stays with Tessaly. Accepting a large loss outright may exceed the board's appetite, zero risk is neither possible nor economic, and avoiding the risk by switching systems off would stop the business it is meant to protect.

ns-0033.why: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, Tessaly must preserve relevant electronically stored information, and a legal hold suspends routine deletion. Civil cases turn on the preponderance of evidence, which makes the record critical. Waiting lets the 90-day rule destroy it, an early purge is spoliation, and ad hoc copies on a laptop break integrity and custody.

ns-0034.why: A compensating control delivers comparable protection when the required control cannot be implemented. MFA enforced at a jump host, allowlisting and session recording bring the risk close to what gateway MFA would, documented and reviewed until replacement. A bare waiver leaves the gap open, stronger passwords are still a single factor, and there is no default exemption for legacy kit.

ns-0035.why: A role change must revoke old access as well as grant new, or privilege creep builds up. Here it has produced a toxic combination: refunds plus treasury. Fix this case and the process that caused it. Keeping rights 'just in case' breaks least privilege, an annual review is too slow to catch the rest, and a second account leaves the same person holding both roles.

ns-0036.why: A continuity plan has to be maintained through change: a major platform move should trigger an update and a fresh test with the process owners. Waiting leaves a plan that fails on the night it is needed. The provider's resilience covers its own infrastructure, not Tessaly's processes, and a contact-only fix leaves recovery steps that point at a data centre that no longer runs anything.

ns-0037.why: A policy's authority comes from senior management. Executive approval signals commitment, allocates resources and turns compliance into a management expectation rather than a request from one department. Re-signing by security changes nothing about its authority, local rewrites fragment the rules, and blocking logins coerces people without giving the policy any legitimacy.

ns-0038.why: Awareness points everyone's attention at risks; training builds role-specific skills, and a good programme is tailored by role. Developers shipping injection flaws need hands-on secure coding training grounded in the OWASP classics. Watching the general module again teaches no new skills, posters are just more awareness, and a one-size programme ignores the people with the most technical risk.

ns-0039.why: An exception process keeps the standard intact while recording a justified deviation: time-bound, accepted by the risk owner, with compensating measures and a review date. A permanent exception quietly becomes the new rule, an undocumented workaround is unmanaged risk, and rewriting the standard for one printer weakens it for everyone.

ns-0040.why: Under GDPR a personal data breach likely to put people at risk must reach the supervisory authority no later than 72 hours after Tessaly becomes aware, and details can follow in phases. Waiting for the full root cause blows the deadline, a leak-site sighting is not the legal test, and an unreviewed mass email may be inaccurate and still does not meet the duty to notify the regulator.

ns-0041.why: The ISC2 Code requires you to act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally. Backdated reviews are falsified records that mislead the assessor, whoever signs them. Report the gap truthfully with a plan to close it and escalate internally if pressure continues. A private note does not undo the falsification, and handing the pen to a colleague just spreads the misconduct.

ns-0042.why: A service-level requirement (SLR) states what the customer needs, such as detection and response times, coverage hours and reporting, and it drives the SLA that is negotiated. Without SLRs you are ranking vendors against each other, not against Tessaly's need. Document length is not coverage, post-go-live negotiation has no leverage, and copying a vendor's terms lets the market set your requirement.

ns-0043.why: When hard data is missing, a qualitative assessment built on informed judgement gives a defensible ranking, and stating its limits keeps the decision honest. A made-up euro figure offers false precision the CFO might act on. No loss history does not mean no risk, and a figure borrowed from a different threat at a different site describes neither.

ns-0044.why: A regulatory investigation is run by a government body under its own authority, and the organisation must comply fully and on time, coordinated through legal. Selective disclosure risks being treated as obstruction. Regulators generally do not need a court order to request records within their remit, and asking for more time does not suspend the obligation to keep collecting.

ns-0045.why: The CIA triad is balanced by business priority, and for card authorisation availability dominates, so a control must not become the outage. Out-of-band inspection still watches the traffic without sitting in its path. Confidentiality does not automatically come first, removing all inspection overcorrects, and stacking inline devices multiplies exactly the latency and failure risk you are trying to avoid.

ns-0046.why: Personnel security reaches third parties through the contract: screening, confidentiality, conduct rules and prompt notice when someone leaves hold the vendor's staff to Tessaly's standard. The employer of record does not change who is exposed. A shared badge destroys accountability, and unescorted access with yearly CCTV review is far too little oversight for a server room.

ns-0047.why: An occupant emergency plan protects people during a physical threat: evacuation routes, shelter, assembly points and accounting for everyone on shift. Human safety always comes before systems. Disaster recovery, incident response and crisis communications plans all matter, but they protect technology and reputation, and none tells a night-shift picker where to go when the alarm sounds.

ns-0048.why: Acquisitions are a governance process, and due diligence must cover security: undisclosed breaches, technical debt and inherited compliance obligations all become Tessaly's on closing. After signing, the liability is already yours. Connecting an unassessed network imports its risk, and a seller warranty may help recover losses later but does not tell you what you are buying.

ns-0049.why: Simulations exist to teach and to build a reporting culture. Private, just-in-time coaching at the moment of the mistake, plus visible praise for reporting, changes behaviour. Public shaming and pay penalties teach staff to hide clicks, which is the worst outcome during a real attack, and a simulation with no follow-up measures people without improving them.

ns-0050.why: A security policy is management's high-level statement of goals, scope and responsibilities, and it should rarely change. Technology-specific detail belongs in standards, baselines and procedures beneath it, which can change without re-approving the policy. Weekly edits to one giant document never end, vendor guides carry no Tessaly authority, and optional guidelines remove the mandate.

ns-0051.why: Software licences are enforceable intellectual property terms, and commercial use under a non-commercial licence is infringement. Bring in legal and either buy the right licence or replace the component. Public availability is not permission, disguising the files turns a mistake into wilful infringement, and attribution satisfies only some licences, never a commercial-use restriction.

ns-0052.why: The first canon of the ISC2 Code is to protect society, the common good and the infrastructure. Coordinated disclosure gets the flaw fixed before attackers learn of it, and going through Tessaly respects your employer's interests. Publishing before a fix exists arms attackers against thousands of firms, silence leaves them exposed, and selling the flaw is dishonourable whatever happens to the money.

ns-0053.why: Supplier risk management needs independent evidence rather than self-attestation, so ask for a SOC 2 Type II or similar. Subprocessors are fourth parties that extend the chain and must be known, and audit rights keep assurance alive after signing. A discount does not reduce exposure, and accountability for staff data stays with Tessaly whatever the contract says.

ns-0054.why: Risk management is continuous. Key risk indicators, such as scanner patch lag, watch for drift between assessments, and thresholds force the owner to act before the next annual cycle. A bigger yearly assessment still leaves eleven blind months, a new tool does not fix a process that never looks, and a known risk that is still growing must stay on the register.

ns-0055.why: A watering hole attack compromises a site a target group trusts, so victims are infected just by visiting. No alerts does not mean no compromise, so hunt retrospectively through proxy logs, examine the hosts that visited, and block the site until it is clean. The forum owner is most likely a victim too, and a vague warning cannot stop scripts that run on page load.

ns-0056.why: Friendly departures still need formal offboarding. An exit interview reminds her of continuing confidentiality obligations, assets come back, and access ends when employment does. Good terms do not make fraud-scoring knowledge less sensitive. Cutting access days early is disproportionate without a specific risk, and having her delete her own mailbox destroys business records.

ns-0057.why: A recovery strategy must deliver an RTO inside the maximum tolerable downtime set by the business impact analysis. A 16-hour gap means the owner must choose and fund a different strategy, such as a warm standby or a manual dispatch workaround. Editing the BIA or the RTO to match current capability turns the process upside down, and hoping is not a strategy.

ns-0058.why: Security governance means setting strategic direction aligned to business objectives, assigning accountability and overseeing results; a steering committee of business leaders does that. An engineers' vote is operations making strategy, an outsourced provider can deliver services but cannot hold Tessaly's accountability, and budget without direction is spending, not governance.

ns-0059.why: Awareness starts at onboarding, before access is granted, and is refreshed at regular intervals afterwards. The first months are when new starters know the least and attackers target them the most. Anyone with a login is a phishing target whatever their job, and clicking a policy link records an event without building any awareness.

ns-0060.why: Every policy needs a named owner and a periodic review so it keeps pace with how the business actually works. A stale rule breeds normalised non-compliance that spreads to other policies. Enforcing an obsolete ban fights the business, an informal licence to ignore rules erodes all of them, and deleting the policy leaves remote work with no rules at all.

ns-0061.why: PCI DSS is an industry standard enforced by contract with the card brands, so it binds Tessaly Pay even though it is not statute. Storing full card numbers pulls the warehouse into scope. Tokenisation keeps analytic value while keeping raw card data out. Copying first and scoping later is a live violation, and a key stored beside its data protects very little.

ns-0062.why: Browsing a customer's records without need breaches privacy and the ISC2 Code, and members are expected to support the Code, including by reporting breaches they witness. Use Tessaly's process first; a formal ISC2 ethics complaint is available if warranted. Friendship does not change the breach, deleting logs destroys evidence and is misconduct itself, and a vague chat post fixes nothing.

ns-0063.why: An SLA turns supplier performance into something measurable and enforceable. A high uptime guarantee matched to the app's need, backed by service credits and termination rights, gives Tessaly leverage it lacked last year. Best efforts means no remedy, continuity accountability cannot be handed to a supplier, and a discount does nothing to reduce the impact of the next outage.

ns-0064.why: Annualised loss expectancy is the single loss expectancy times the annual rate of occurrence: $120,000 × 0.25 = $30,000. That is the ceiling for yearly spend on the risk; paying more costs more than the loss it prevents. The single-loss figure is per event, not per year, multiplying by four inverts the rate, and an infrequent loss still carries an expected annual cost.

ns-0065.why: A business impact analysis must map dependencies, including third parties, because that is where hidden single points of failure live. Once the provider is rated, continuity strategy can supply an alternate channel such as an authenticator app. Internal-only scope misses exactly this risk, cancelling the provider breaks the processes, and the supplier's plan protects the supplier, not Tessaly.

ns-0066.why: A recognised control framework, such as an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS or the NIST CSF, gives governance a structure: one managed control set, mapped once to many external demands. Answering from scratch wastes effort and yields inconsistent claims. A tool's default checklist lets a vendor define your controls, and a home-grown framework is harder for auditors and customers to trust.

ns-0067.why: An acceptable use policy sets out what staff may and may not do with company equipment, and a signed acknowledgement makes it enforceable. Disciplining someone for breaking an unwritten rule is unfair and hard to defend. Locking tablets without explanation creates workarounds and resentment, and a guideline is optional by definition, so it gives HR nothing to enforce.

ns-0068.why: Divestitures are a governance process too: data must be split under agreed terms, identities migrated, and every shared trust path removed by an agreed date, with transitional access tightly limited. Admin rights on the directory hand another company the keys to Tessaly, open-ended shared links leave a permanent back door, and deleting data the buyer has paid for breaches the deal.

ns-0069.why: Once residual risk falls within appetite, the right move is formal acceptance by the risk owner, with monitoring in case conditions change. More controls past that point spend money beyond the value they protect. Accepted risks stay on the register and are watched, and paying to transfer a risk the board has already said it can live with is wasted premium.

ns-0070.why: The gap is detection. Preventive controls will eventually be bypassed, so defence in depth layers a detective control behind them: a daily reconciliation catches the refund that slipped past approval. Another approver strengthens the layer that already exists, a warning banner is a deterrent, and restoring deleted records is a recovery control that never notices the fraud.

ns-0071.why: Purpose limitation means personal data collected for one purpose cannot simply be reused for an incompatible one. Publicly ranking employees from location data is a new, intrusive purpose that needs its own lawful basis and a data protection impact assessment. Lawfully holding the data for safety does not cover marketing, first names still identify drivers, and a retroactive notice is too late.

ns-0072.why: Controls are selected to treat assessed risks, so governance starts with a risk assessment of the markets' threats, laws, fraud patterns and cash handling. Copying the home market's controls assumes identical risks, a competitor's marketing tells you nothing about Tessaly's exposure, and waiting for losses to reveal the gaps makes customers and staff pay for the analysis.

ns-0073.why: Single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor: $900,000 × 0.35 = $315,000. The exposure factor is the share of value lost in one event, so the full asset value overstates the loss, and treating 35% as a dollar figure or dividing by it confuses the formula. The SLE later feeds the annualised loss expectancy once a rate of occurrence is known.

ns-0074.why: Cryptography is subject to export and import controls, under the Wassenaar Arrangement and national law, and some destinations need licences or ban certain products. Legal must clear the shipment first. Availability online is not a licence, removing encryption leaves the office's data exposed, and routing through a third country is deliberate evasion of the law.

ns-0075.why: NIS2 covers transport among its sectors and requires essential entities to report significant incidents in stages: an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours, and a final report within a month. Assuming the directive is limited to energy and health is wrong, media coverage is not the threshold, and a yearly summary misses every statutory deadline.

ns-0076.why: Failed SSDs often cannot be overwritten or verified, so physical destruction on site (with a keep-your-drive clause and a certificate) is the only disposal that guarantees the data is gone. A vendor promise shifts the risk without controlling it, and a format on a dead drive does nothing; dropping warranties treats cost, not the data exposure.

ns-0077.why: A per-recipient digital watermark ties each leaked copy back to its source, which deters leaks and makes attribution possible next time. A PDF is still trivially copied, a new NDA adds no way to prove who breached it, and halting all sharing breaks the business process instead of protecting the asset inside it.

ns-0078.why: A legal hold overrides the normal destruction stage of the data lifecycle: once litigation is reasonably expected, deleting relevant records is spoliation. Letting the scheduled purge run ignores that duty, a personal copy breaks custody and handling rules, and deliberate deletion is obstruction, the worst outcome for the company.

ns-0079.why: Containing the exposure while preserving the access logs lets you judge what was taken and whether breach notification applies; the data owner decides next steps. Deleting the bucket destroys the evidence of exposure, waiting until morning leaves customer data public, and blocking two IPs does nothing about the rest of the internet.

ns-0080.why: Card data is decrypted in RAM while it is processed, so disk and transport encryption do nothing against memory scraping: data in use needs its own protection. Isolating and capturing memory contains the attack and keeps evidence. Rebooting wipes that volatile evidence, and rotating a certificate protects the wrong data state.

ns-0081.why: Secret marks information whose disclosure would do serious damage, so containment comes first: restore need-to-know and alert the owner, who judges the impact. Classification reflects value, not current exposure, so downgrading it hides the incident. A mass email advertises the leak, and withholding logs from the owner undermines the response.

ns-0082.why: Backup retention must outlast the likely dwell time; here only the offline monthly archive predates the intrusion, so it is the clean recovery point, then you replay newer data after checks. Last night's backup probably carries the implant, paying funds crime without a guarantee, and an empty rebuild throws away recoverable records.

ns-0083.why: Test environments are rarely hardened, so the lasting fix is de-identification: masked or synthetic records keep the data useful for debugging while removing the link to real people. Disk encryption does not help once the host is compromised and running, a ticket leaves live data in test, and deleting afterwards still exposes it during use.

ns-0084.why: Data location is a lifecycle control: storing records outside the agreed jurisdiction breaches residency commitments. Pause first to stop the spread, preserve a record of what moved, and let the privacy lead decide on remediation and notification. Letting it finish widens the breach, encryption does not change where it sits, and deleting logs destroys evidence.

ns-0085.why: Encryption with keys kept apart from the data can turn a stolen file into unreadable ciphertext, which legal can weigh against notification rules; but that holds only if the keys were not exposed, so verify and rotate. Saying nothing was lost ignores the unencrypted fields, and wiping the server destroys the forensic trail.

ns-0086.why: Asset value, recorded in the inventory and classification, drives protection and response priority: the signed contracts carry far more business impact than a dev wiki, and mass renames suggest active encryption. First-come order ignores impact, splitting one responder slows both, and waiting lets the damage grow.

ns-0087.why: Formatting rebuilds the file system tables but leaves the data blocks, so the drives are not sanitised. Holding the pickup and purging or destroying each drive, with a record, meets disposal requirements. A contract clause is not verification, a second format has the same flaw, and one sample proves the whole batch is exposed.

ns-0088.why: Handling requirements set how classified media is moved: approved carriers, tamper-evident packaging and a custody log, so loss can be detected and traced. Encryption reduces impact but does not waive handling rules, an unlogged personal trip breaks custody, and holding the tapes on site defeats the point of offsite backup.

ns-0089.why: Deleting files only removes the pointers to them; the data stays on the disk and is easily recovered, which is data remanence. Overwriting with a verified tool clears the media for reuse within the company. Emptying the bin changes nothing on disk, renaming is cosmetic, and an AUP does not grant lab staff need-to-know.

ns-0090.why: Data in transit over plain FTP exposes both the files and the credentials to anyone on the path; SFTP encrypts the channel and key authentication removes the shared password. Rotating a password that still crosses in cleartext solves nothing, legacy zip passwords are weak, and a quiet history is not a risk assessment.

ns-0091.why: The data owner, a business leader accountable for the data, sets its classification; custodians such as the storage team and the SOC implement the controls that follow. Picking a level yourself takes a decision that is not yours, over-classifying wastes budget and slows use, and letting the custodian choose inverts accountability.

ns-0092.why: For reuse inside the organisation at the same sensitivity, overwriting (clearing) is proportionate: it defeats ordinary recovery and keeps the drives in service. Shredding is for media leaving control or failing verification, a quick format leaves data behind, and degaussing a modern HDD wipes its servo tracks, so the drive is useless.

ns-0093.why: This is improper asset handling: sensitive data on unmarked, unencrypted media in an open drawer. Secure the media, record it as an incident so the owner can judge exposure, and replace the habit with an approved transfer method. Wiping destroys evidence, relocking keeps the broken process, and silent disposal fixes nothing that caused it.

ns-0094.why: Data minimisation starts at collection, the first stage of the lifecycle: gather only what a stated purpose needs, so there is less to protect, retain and lose. Encrypting unneeded data still means holding it, optional fields still invite sensitive data you have no reason to keep, and a review a year later is after the harm.

ns-0095.why: Personal information includes any data that can identify a person directly or indirectly; van ID plus the roster pins a trace to a driver's movements. That triggers privacy obligations, so a privacy impact assessment decides the lawful basis and safeguards. The roster still exists elsewhere, and a blanket ban ignores legitimate, controlled use.

ns-0096.why: You cannot protect what you have not inventoried: recording the asset and assigning an owner is what lets its data be classified and given proper controls and retention. Wiping an unowned server may destroy records the business must keep, ignoring it leaves an unmanaged risk, and an agent alone does not settle ownership or classification.

ns-0097.why: Record retention is set by legal and regulatory duty plus business need: keep for the mandated period, then destroy on schedule. Keeping forever grows storage cost, breach impact and discovery exposure; 90 days breaks customs law; and local choice makes the schedule unenforceable and inconsistent across depots.

ns-0098.why: Labelling media with its classification tells every handler, including third parties, what care it needs: payment tapes get stricter storage, transport and destruction than marketing ones. Encryption does not tell anyone how to handle or dispose of the tape, separation without labels depends on memory, and a false Public marking invites mishandling.

ns-0099.why: Tessaly stays the data controller; the provider is a processor that may act only on documented instructions. The agreement must limit use, govern sub-processors and fix deletion at contract end. Signing first hands away the leverage, assuming the processor carries the duty is wrong, and a policy after go-live is too late.

ns-0100.why: Proper data encryption uses vetted, public algorithms with keys managed outside the code; a secret design with a hardcoded key is broken the moment anyone reverses the app. Moving the key to a config file on the same device changes nothing, XOR twice with one key undoes itself, and secrecy of the design is not strength.

ns-0101.why: Aggregation can make combined data more sensitive than any part: addresses plus cash schedules plus guard rotas is a robbery plan. The combined set needs its own, higher classification and tighter access, decided by the owners. Inheriting the lowest label ignores that, device limits do not fix the label, and a blanket ban blocks legitimate analysis.

ns-0102.why: Asset retention includes tracking end-of-life and end-of-support dates so owners can budget and replace before vendor patches stop. Recording the dates with advance alerts turns a surprise into a planned decision. Unofficial patches add supply chain risk, waiting a quarter leaves them unpatched, and blanket extended support wastes money.

ns-0103.why: Where no law sets a period, retention follows business requirements, decided by the data owner: here the dispute window plus a margin. Keeping photos forever adds cost and exposure with no benefit, a week breaks the dispute process, and a vendor's pricing is not a business requirement.

ns-0104.why: Secure storage separates the media from the keys and puts each under access control: drives in a locked safe, recovery keys in the managed key vault. Keys beside the ciphertext cancel the encryption, discarding the only recovery keys risks losing the archive, and a different desk is still open-plan.

ns-0105.why: Classification should change as value and sensitivity change, but declassification is the owner's decision and must be recorded so handling rules update everywhere. The SOC is not the owner, never downgrading wastes effort protecting public data, and publishing before the record changes breaks the handling policy.

ns-0106.why: Secure provisioning means an asset is recorded, owned and hardened before it touches data: inventory, device management and a baseline image give you patching, encryption and remote wipe from day one. Setup later leaves unmanaged devices on live data, local admin undermines the baseline, and self-reported serials make inventory unreliable.

ns-0107.why: Scoping and tailoring adapt a baseline to a system: drop controls that do not apply, add or substitute where needed, and document the rationale so assessors can follow it. Forcing unworkable controls wastes effort, skipping the whole baseline leaves the kiosks ungoverned, and a separate unlinked baseline breaks traceability.

ns-0108.why: Uncontrolled copies break the data lifecycle: each needs protecting, retention and disposal, and conflicting versions damage integrity. One system of record, reconciled then enforced, fixes both. Keeping them multiplies exposure (backups are for loss), encryption leaves the integrity mess, and deleting without reconciling throws away the banking changes.

ns-0109.why: The asset retention policy exists so devices that may hold evidence are kept intact for the set period; sealing and storing preserves it for any legal claim. Reimaging destroys evidence, a partial copy misses local files and metadata and breaks custody, and the former team has neither authority nor independence.

ns-0110.why: Handling requirements cover output as well as storage: secure print release holds the job until the authorised person is present, so Confidential pages never sit unattended. Moving the printer still leaves overnight piles for cleaners and visitors, a sign is not a control, and banning print ignores why the team needs paper.

ns-0111.why: A system is categorised by the high-water mark: the most sensitive data it holds sets the protection level, because a breach of the platform exposes everything on it. Rating by traffic volume or averaging understates the ledger's impact, and per-page ratings ignore the shared infrastructure an attacker would actually compromise.

ns-0112.why: Data loss prevention inspects content leaving the organisation and can block or quarantine card numbers in outbound email, addressing the channel that failed. A reminder helps awareness but enforces nothing, blocking webmail at the proxy does not stop company mail sent to outside addresses, and punishment does not create a control.

ns-0113.why: Cryptographic erase destroys the media encryption key on a self-encrypting drive, making the data unrecoverable while leaving the drive usable: the right end-of-life move when drives must be returned. Overwrites are unreliable on SSDs because of wear levelling, a format leaves data, and shredding breaches the lease at needless cost.

ns-0114.why: Tokenisation replaces card numbers with tokens that are useless if stolen, so CRM and dispatch drop out of scope and billing charges via the vault. Encryption with a shared key keeps all three in scope, since each can decrypt; an expiry date alone cannot recognise or charge a card; and a firewall does not shrink the data footprint.

ns-0115.why: Compliance requirements follow the data: you must know what personal data flows where, and which laws, regulators and standards apply, before choosing controls. Assuming parity misses local rules, waiting for a regulator is non-compliance by design, and a tool cannot tell you what your obligations are without that mapping.

ns-0116.why: A cloud access security broker gives visibility of shadow SaaS use and applies data policy (allow, block, or protect uploads) between users and cloud services. Blocking everything breaks approved work and drives workarounds, self-reported lists miss the problem, and a bigger share without enforcement changes nothing.

ns-0117.why: Digital rights management keeps the controls attached to the file wherever it goes, enforcing view, print, forward and expiry rights on the recipient's device. Encrypted email protects transit only, an expiring link does nothing once the file is downloaded, and a marking relies on goodwill instead of enforcement.

ns-0118.why: Full disk encryption protects every file at rest on a lost or stolen device, including temp files and swap, and with pre-boot unlock and central key escrow the data is unreadable when powered off. A login password is bypassed by pulling the drive, folder encryption misses copies elsewhere, and a cable lock only slows a thief.

ns-0119.why: A security baseline, drawn from a published benchmark and tailored where needed, sets one minimum configuration that can be deployed and audited consistently. Documenting current habits bakes in the gaps, annual reviews leave drift unmanaged, and a scanner finds problems but gives no standard for how servers should be built.

ns-0120.why: Data masking shows each role only what it needs: agents confirm the last four digits while the full number stays hidden, applying least privilege to the data itself. Logging detects misuse after the fact, removing the field entirely breaks the verification task, and a pledge is not a technical control.

ns-0121.why: Encryption is only as strong as its key management: keys stored beside the data, readable by the same people, give an attacker or insider both at once. A managed key service with separation of duties keeps keys out of DBA reach and logs their use. Another local key repeats the flaw, renaming is obscurity, and rotation leaves them exposed.

ns-0122.why: This is an integrity risk: a digital signature proves the file came from the payments system and has not been altered, and the uploader can refuse any file that fails verification. Disk encryption protects confidentiality, not changes by authorised folder users, timestamps are easily forged, and a matching total misses a swapped account number.

ns-0123.why: When a required control cannot be met, a compensating control that meets the intent (network isolation and application allowlisting here) is documented, risk-assessed and accepted by the owner. Forcing the agent risks outage and lost support, recording false compliance is misrepresentation, and hiding the asset leaves the risk and adds dishonesty.

ns-0124.why: Polyinstantiation lets the same key exist at several classification levels with different values, so the clerk sees a plausible record and the inference channel closes. Rewording the error fails the moment a clerk tries to create that ID and hits a key collision; a detached database breaks operations; training cannot close a technical inference channel.

ns-0125.why: A capacitance detector sets an electrical field around one object and alarms when a body disturbs it, so it guards the cabinet whatever the room's airflow does. Raising motion sensitivity brings back the false alarms that got the sensors tuned down; morning footage review is detective and too late; a desk drawer is weaker storage, not better detection.

ns-0126.why: Identical, validly signed copies from a new source are a replay attack: a genuine message captured and resent, no key needed. Containing the source and rejecting repeated or stale messages with nonces and timestamps stops it. Rotating the key or strengthening the algorithm misses the point, because nothing was forged; letting them through pays the batch three times.

ns-0127.why: In a community cloud, organisations with a shared mission share the infrastructure and its governance, so incident duties sit in the community agreement: invoke it and contain Tessaly's own exposure. Scanning hosts you don't own is unauthorised testing; waiting ignores Tessaly's duty to its data; walking off the platform mid-incident is a business decision, not containment.

ns-0128.why: Applications belong in ring 3, user mode, where the processor stops them touching the kernel or other processes' memory; that boundary is what is blocking this suspicious write. Moving the code into ring 0 or granting admin hands a possibly compromised program full control of the host; disabling the rule removes the only alarm you have.

ns-0129.why: A fixed shift is a Caesar-style substitution cipher: with only a few dozen possible keys it falls to brute force or frequency analysis in seconds, so the PINs were effectively plaintext. Reset them and move to a vetted algorithm. A new shift value or a second shift is still one trivial substitution; silencing the researcher changes nothing about the exposure.

ns-0130.why: Life safety outranks asset protection: egress doors are designed to fail safe so people can escape a fire, and the cameras keep tracking the visitor for police. Holding doors locked could trap staff in a real fire and breaches fire code; silencing the alarm or sending staff to confront an unknown person trades people's safety for an arrest.

ns-0131.why: Industrial controllers often cannot be patched or run agents, so the mitigation is architectural: contain the source, then segment OT from office IT so only engineering hosts can reach them. Beta firmware on live, safety-relevant kit risks the line and the people near it; PLCs rarely support antivirus; shutting the hub for months is disproportionate.

ns-0132.why: Differentiated security controls match protection to the sensitivity of each part of a system: payment data gets step-up MFA while public tracking stays frictionless. Blanket MFA taxes low-risk uses and drives customers away; taking the portal down hurts everyone; a single CAPTCHA keeps one-size-fits-all protection in front of the card data.

ns-0133.why: Biba's simple integrity property says a high-integrity subject must not read from a lower-integrity source ('no read down'), because unvetted input contaminates trusted output. Cut the feed, then correct the tainted runs. Range checks still let bad data in; flagging passes the problem to customers; encrypting the feed protects its transit, not its trustworthiness.

ns-0134.why: A UPS buys time for an orderly response, not continuity; the facility's shutdown plan sheds low-priority load so critical systems last longer and nothing crashes uncontrolled. Retrying and waiting on the utility gamble the whole room on the clock; dropping everything at once takes down payment services the remaining battery could still carry.

ns-0135.why: A collision attack, powered by the birthday paradox, lets an attacker craft a different file with the same MD5 digest, so the checksum no longer proves identity. Pause and move to a collision-resistant hash under a signature. Republishing or re-checking the same MD5 verifies nothing new; matching digests are exactly what the attacker engineered.

ns-0136.why: Fail securely: when a control cannot decide, the system should default to deny and queue the work, not grant it. Allow-on-timeout means anyone who can overload the service can pay themselves. Scaling out is sensible later but leaves the door open tonight; removing the check turns a temporary failure into a deliberate one.

ns-0137.why: The control unit directs how the CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions, so a flaw there sits below every operating system: it needs vendor microcode, and meanwhile sensitive workloads get their own hardware. Guest OS patches cannot fix the processor; disk encryption does not help because the leak happens in memory while data is in use.

ns-0138.why: Once a private key is exposed, trust in its certificate is gone; revocation publishes that through CRL and OCSP so clients stop accepting it, and a fresh key pair restores service. Deleting the commit cannot recall copies already cloned or cached; validity dates say nothing about compromise; a contractor's assurance is not evidence.

ns-0139.why: Flash media is not magnetic, so degaussing leaves the data intact, and failed drives often still hold readable chips. For card data the dependable end is witnessed physical destruction such as shredding or incineration, with a certificate. A quick format only rewrites the file table; assuming a dead drive is unreadable is how media leaks happen.

ns-0140.why: A federated or consortium blockchain is permissioned: a known group of members validates, and membership and keys are managed through that shared governance. So the response runs through the consortium, which can revoke and reissue. Assuming one node is harmless ignores that the stolen key signs as Tessaly; a local fork abandons the shared ledger; public forums are the wrong channel.

ns-0141.why: Link encryption encrypts everything on the link, headers included, so the carrier sees neither content nor which hosts converse. Application TLS is end-to-end: it protects payloads but leaves IP headers and routing readable. Hashing is not encryption and the receiver cannot reverse it; a contract clause is an administrative promise, not a technical control.

ns-0142.why: The Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) model grants access dynamically: once an analyst touches one client's data, competing clients in the same conflict class become off-limits, preventing conflicts of interest. A shared classification label cannot express 'rivals'; logging only detects after the leak; separate keys handed to the same person enforce nothing.

ns-0143.why: This is aggregation: individually low-sensitivity data combines into something sensitive, so the collection must be judged at the higher level. Dropping or generalising the fields that enable the inference fixes it. Field-by-field classification misses the combination; promises and PDF formats do not stop anyone combining data once they hold it.

ns-0144.why: Layered physical defence in depth puts several independent barriers, detection and delay between an intruder and the asset, so one failure, a tailgater or a propped door, does not expose everything. One premium lock is a single point of failure; two locks on one door are still one layer; disk encryption complements physical security but does not stop tampering before imaging.

ns-0145.why: A TPM records measurements of firmware and boot components in its PCRs and can seal a key so it unseals only when those measurements match, so a tampered boot chain simply gets no key. A password in the boot script is readable by anyone with the disk; a USB stick relies on people and travels; a weekly scan is detective and runs after a compromised boot.

ns-0146.why: This is a timing side-channel attack: the algorithm is fine, but the implementation leaks information through how long it takes. A constant-time comparison removes the signal. A bigger key or new algorithm never touches the leak; longer tokens only slow the per-character attack; random delays add noise that averaging over many requests filters out.

ns-0147.why: Edge computing moves processing close to where data is produced, cutting latency and link dependency but spreading assets into less-protected places. So each edge node needs hardening, central configuration and patching, and encryption for the data it holds. Printer-grade treatment or per-site settings create drift; flat rejection blocks a legitimate need that should be enabled securely.

ns-0148.why: ECDSA depends on a unique, unpredictable nonce for every signature; if two signatures share one, the private key can be calculated from them, HSM or not. Generate it properly, with strong randomness or RFC 6979 derivation. The HSM protects key storage, not the maths; a longer curve leaks just the same; signing less only slows the leak.

ns-0149.why: The Take-Grant model treats authorisation as a graph: create gives a subject full rights over the new object, and grant passes rights on, so a creating subject becomes a route for rights to spread anywhere. Gating grants keeps creation useful while stopping uncontrolled propagation. 'Only its own buckets' is exactly the route; manual creation overcorrects; quarterly review detects too late.

ns-0150.why: This is a time-of-check to time-of-use race: state changes between the check and the use. Making the check and payout one atomic transaction under a lock closes the window. A check after payout is only detective; per-account rate limits narrow the window but parallel sessions still slip through; logging only helps chase the money afterwards.

ns-0151.why: Data execution prevention marks data pages non-executable and ASLR randomises memory layout, together blunting most memory-corruption exploits. When a legacy component cannot live with them, isolate it so the exception is contained until replacement. Disabling them host-wide exposes every service; half-disabling still weakens the host; breaking the workflow ignores a real business need.

ns-0152.why: A downgrade attack forces both sides onto the weakest protocol they still share, then breaks that. Removing legacy versions and weak cipher suites at both ends leaves nothing to fall back to. Keeping fallback preserves the hole; hiding the network name does not stop a rogue access point; an extra password does nothing for the channel's cryptography.

ns-0153.why: Secure defaults and minimal functionality mean a system starts locked down and features are enabled deliberately, so nothing ships exposed by accident. 'Later' rarely comes, and a demo account or public SNMP string is an easy first foothold. A firewall helps, but insiders and anything moving laterally still reach the open services.

ns-0154.why: Only a digital signature made with a private key held by one person gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation together. An HMAC proves integrity and that someone holding the shared key sent it, but any manager could have, so nobody can be held to it. Longer keys and timestamps do not change that; encrypting to finance gives confidentiality, not proof of origin.

ns-0155.why: Bell-LaPadula's simple security property is 'no read up': a subject may not read an object classified above its clearance, because reading is exactly how confidentiality is lost, so read-only is irrelevant. Seniority is not clearance; watermarks deter onward sharing but still hand over the content. A cleared investigator meets the need without breaking the model.

ns-0156.why: Semantic integrity means the database enforces that values make sense for their field, such as types, ranges and plausible dates, and rejects the rest at write time, whatever the source. Encryption protects transit, but these values were wrong at the scanner; manual checks do not scale and miss things; restoring old backups throws away good data with the bad.

ns-0157.why: EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light through its window and then rewritten with a programmer, so the attack path is physical: someone must expose or pull the chip. Tamper-evident seals and inspection cover that path. These boards have no remote update channel to protect; 'never changed' confuses EPROM with mask ROM; routine chip swaps add handling risk with no integrity check.

ns-0158.why: Secure design pushes security into the earliest phase: threat modelling, for example STRIDE against the data flows, finds design flaws while they are cheap to change. A launch-week pen test finds them when fixing means delay or risk acceptance; a scanner hunts known bug patterns, not design flaws; a signed statement is assurance on paper only.

ns-0159.why: Key recovery, or escrow, keeps a protected copy of keys so the organisation can reach its own data when a person leaves, and dual control stops any single administrator misusing it. Emailed passphrases leak and break accountability; optional backups fail exactly when needed; dropping encryption swaps an availability problem for a confidentiality one.

ns-0160.why: Biba's star integrity property is 'no write up': a lower-integrity subject must not modify a higher-integrity object. Routing kiosk input through validation by a trusted engineer keeps the master register clean. A nightly clean-up lets bad entries be used meanwhile; a typed staff number is not authentication; staffed hours do not change the kiosk's integrity level.

ns-0161.why: The hypervisor is the most privileged component in the estate, so its management plane must be isolated: a compromised guest that reaches it can own every VM. VM sprawl, unowned and unpatched machines, needs inventory and retirement. Patching alone leaves the management plane exposed; host antivirus does not fix the architecture; snapshots help recovery but prevent nothing.

ns-0162.why: Zero trust drops the idea that being inside the network earns trust: every request is authenticated and authorised on identity, device and context, to specific resources only. An encrypted tunnel protects transit but still hands over the whole network; a company laptop helps posture but not scope; monthly review is detective and late.

ns-0163.why: An IPsec security association is one-way: it binds one direction of traffic to its keys, algorithms and SPI, so a two-way tunnel needs a pair, inbound and outbound. Reusing one SPI or lengthening a key does not change that; plain GRE carries traffic with no encryption at all, removing the protection the processor requires.

ns-0164.why: Clark-Wilson protects integrity by never letting users touch constrained data directly: they work through well-formed transactions that validate input, enforce separation of duties and write an audit trail, the access triple of user, program and data. Scoping the client still allows unvalidated edits; restoring afterwards is reactive; a shared login destroys accountability.

ns-0165.why: Screen-scraping malware captures what the display shows, sidestepping database and transport encryption, because data must be decrypted to be rendered. Masking PANs so the full number never appears removes what it could capture. Encryption at rest is irrelevant to a screenshot; a vendor's self-scan is not your control; a second tool doubles the attack surface.

ns-0166.why: Privacy by design builds data minimisation, purpose limitation and retention limits in from the start, backed by a privacy impact assessment, rather than bolting them on. Encryption protects stored data but does not justify collecting it; employee waivers are weak consent given the power imbalance; waiting for complaints means the over-collection has already happened.

ns-0167.why: Split knowledge means no one person ever holds the whole key, and dual control means custodians must act together, so a master key cannot be stolen or misused by one insider. A safe improves storage but keeps the single-person risk; emailing a key spreads it in plaintext across mail systems; no backup risks losing every protected key if the HSM fails.

ns-0168.why: Bell-LaPadula's star security property is 'no write down': a subject working at a higher level must not write to a lower one, because that is how classified content leaks, deliberately or through a Trojan. The user's clearance is irrelevant; the destination's level is what matters. Stripping headers relabels rather than declassifies; a weekly DLP scan finds leaks after they are readable.

ns-0169.why: A hard-coded login that bypasses authentication is a back door, or maintenance hook: access outside normal controls that anyone who finds it can use. Require its removal and give the vendor managed, logged, time-bound support access instead. Accepting or merely registering it leaves the bypass live; an IP restriction still trusts the vendor's whole network and hides the flaw.

ns-0170.why: Under the shared responsibility model for IaaS, the provider secures the facility, hardware and hypervisor, but the customer still owns the guest OS, patching, configuration, data and identity. A matrix makes those duties explicit. Provider certifications cover only the provider's layers; IaaS providers do not patch your guest OS; running the old system forever is not a security plan.

ns-0171.why: Perfect forward secrecy uses ephemeral key exchange, ECDHE or DHE, so each session key is discarded and cannot be derived from the long-term server key; a stolen key then decrypts nothing already recorded. A longer RSA key or yearly rotation still exposes every session recorded under that key, and the attacker's recordings are not the ones you hold.

ns-0172.why: Embedded and IoT devices often ship with shared default credentials, weak update paths and exposed consoles; the mitigations are unique credentials, network isolation and a firmware maintenance process. 'No sensitive data' ignores that a thermostat is a foothold and that cold-storage temperatures are an availability and safety matter; the main network puts that foothold next to everything else.

ns-0173.why: Keep it simple, or economy of mechanism: security logic small and clear enough to review and test has fewer hidden gaps. Overlapping filters nobody can diagram hide inconsistencies attackers exploit. Defence in depth means independent layers, not tangled duplicates of one control, and delivery speed is not a security criterion.

ns-0174.why: Elliptic curve cryptography reaches roughly the strength of RSA-3072 with a 256-bit key, so it needs less memory, bandwidth and power, which suits constrained devices. RSA-3072 works but strains the chip; RSA-1024 is too weak for new designs; one shared symmetric key across every tag means a single extracted tag compromises the fleet.

ns-0175.why: In PaaS the provider runs the OS and runtime, but configuration, secrets, identity and network exposure stay with the customer. Managed identity or a vault removes the stored secret, and access rules shrink the attack surface. Assuming the provider covers it is the classic misconfiguration; rotation still leaves a readable secret; retreating on-premises discards a platform that can be secured.

ns-0176.why: Multi-cloud improves resilience but multiplies consoles, identity systems and default settings, so controls drift unless policy, identity federation and logging are unified across providers. Provider defaults differ and leave gaps; a weakly secured 'backup' cloud becomes the easy target; a third provider multiplies the same management problem.

ns-0177.why: Symmetric algorithms such as AES are fast enough for bulk data, while asymmetric ones like RSA are far too slow and size-limited for terabytes. The standard pattern is hybrid: AES encrypts the data and RSA protects only the small key. Hashing proves integrity but hides nothing; compression is not confidentiality; a longer window treats the symptom of the wrong tool.

ns-0178.why: Containers share the host kernel, so running as root turns a container escape into a host takeover, and unpinned public images let unvetted changes in at every build. Pinned, scanned images from a trusted registry plus non-root, least-privilege containers fix both. 'Latest' can also mean newly broken; host scans do not fix the image; a bigger host changes nothing.

ns-0179.why: Triple DES runs DES three times, but its 64-bit block and limited effective strength led NIST to deprecate and retire it; AES is the replacement. A dated migration plan, built on crypto agility, is the managed response. Single DES is broken outright; 'unbreakable' is exactly the wrong belief; waiting for a breach accepts a known weakness.

ns-0180.why: Pass-the-hash reuses a captured password hash without cracking it, so one shared local admin hash opens every PC and a cached domain admin hash opens the domain. Unique per-machine passwords and tiered admin that keeps privileged accounts off workstations break that lateral movement. A longer shared password still yields one reusable hash; disk encryption does not protect hashes in memory.

ns-0181.why: Every key needs a defined cryptoperiod, limiting how much data and time an exposure would cover. Envelope encryption, with data keys wrapped under a rotatable key-encryption key, makes rotation cheap. Never rotating accepts unbounded exposure; deleting the old key before re-encryption makes the records permanently unreadable; a fingerprint says nothing about key age.

ns-0182.why: Key stretching makes each guess deliberately expensive: salted, iterated or memory-hard functions such as Argon2, bcrypt or PBKDF2 turn a fast offline cracking run into years. A single fast hash, SHA-256 or SHA-512, can be tested billions of times a second; encrypting the column fails if the key sits beside it; reversible storage means one breach exposes every password.

ns-0183.why: Each IPsec security association carries its keys, algorithms and a lifetime; when it expires, IKE negotiates a new SA with fresh keys, limiting how much traffic any one key protects. Disabling lifetimes leaves one key guarding a year of traffic. Changing the pre-shared key does not refresh SAs already in use; a second tunnel adds availability, not key freshness.

ns-0184.why: Least privilege gives each user and process only the rights its task needs; granting the two apps specific write permission meets the requirement without making every user an administrator. Blanket admin lets any phishing payload install and persist; antivirus is a detective backstop, not a substitute; a shared password destroys accountability.

ns-0185.why: The noninterference model says actions at a higher level must produce no effect a lower-level user can observe; here the fraud job leaks its schedule through a timing covert channel. Separating resources removes the effect. Encryption protects content, but the leak is timing; a warning does not close a channel; a faster report only narrows it.

ns-0186.why: Segmentation with default deny is defense in depth at the network layer: a compromised depot device can no longer reach payment systems at all, shrinking the blast radius. A detection appliance only watches the same flat path being used again, and a password reset treats one symptom while the architecture that allowed the pivot stays unchanged.

ns-0187.why: A rogue access point is a component nobody approved sitting inside the perimeter. Wireless intrusion prevention detects and contains unauthorised radios, and 802.1X port authentication stops an unknown device getting a live wired link in the first place. Hiding the SSID is not a control, since hidden networks are trivially discovered, and a memo alone relies on goodwill instead of enforcement.

ns-0188.why: Certificate validation is what lets partners authenticate the gateway; without it the channel is open to interception. An emergency change restores a trusted certificate while keeping the change record. Turning validation off, or asking partners to blindly trust a self-signed certificate, trains every connected system to accept an impostor, and plain HTTP removes confidentiality and integrity outright.

ns-0189.why: This is a BGP route hijack: the traffic is diverted before it ever reaches Tessaly, so only upstream providers can filter the bad route now. Publishing route origin authorisations through ARIN, the regional internet registry holding the allocation, lets networks using RPKI reject invalid origins in future. A perimeter firewall rule never sees the diverted packets, and registries do not police routing tables.

ns-0190.why: Flooding the MAC table makes a switch fail open and behave like a hub, so every frame can be sniffed. Shutting the port contains the source, and port security limits how many addresses a port may learn, which prevents a repeat. A reboot clears the table only until the flood refills it, and a new VLAN still carries the same port.

ns-0191.why: Telnet sends credentials in cleartext, so anyone capturing on that segment has probably eavesdropped on them already: rotation is required. SSH encrypts the session, and an isolated management network keeps admin traffic away from general hosts. Weekly rotation still sends each new password in the clear, and removing the tool ignores what it has already captured.

ns-0192.why: Long random subdomains sent directly to an outside resolver are the signature of DNS tunnelling for exfiltration. Forcing all resolution through internal resolvers and denying direct outbound DNS contains the channel and gives you logs to inspect. A watchlist leaves data leaving for a week, and caching changes nothing because every tunnelled query is unique.

ns-0193.why: A stateful packet filter judges addresses, ports and session state; it cannot read what is inside an HTTP request. An application-layer proxy firewall terminates the connection and inspects the content, so injection payloads can be blocked while real carriers keep working. Closing 443 turns an attack into a self-inflicted outage, and source ports are random, so rules on them block nothing.

ns-0194.why: Impossible travel on a remote-access tunnel means stolen credentials inside the network. Terminating the session and disabling the account contains it, and multi-factor authentication on the VPN concentrator stops a password alone opening the channel again. Watching lets data leave, waiting on a sleeping user wastes the window, and geo-blocking is bypassed by switching exit nodes.

ns-0195.why: Modern operating systems run IPv6 by default, so rogue router advertisements let an attacker become the gateway for all IPv6 traffic, a man-in-the-middle position. Isolating the host contains it; RA Guard on the switches blocks unauthorised advertisements, and governing IPv6 like IPv4 closes the blind spot. Ignoring it because it is officially unused is exactly how the gap arose.

ns-0196.why: Network access control exists for this: it moves an unknown device to a quarantine VLAN, containing it on that one port while you collect the details to investigate. Shutting every port punishes the whole depot for one device, letting the scan run widens exposure, and a remote wipe cannot work on a laptop that was never enrolled in device management.

ns-0197.why: Gratuitous ARP replies claiming the gateway place the workstation in the middle of the traffic, a man-in-the-middle interception. Isolating it contains the attack, and dynamic ARP inspection validates ARP against trusted bindings so the poisoning cannot recur. Clearing caches or restarting the router lasts only until the next forged reply, and a static route works at the wrong layer.

ns-0198.why: Ethernet frames carry no time-to-live, so a layer-2 loop circulates broadcasts until links saturate. Removing the loop stops the storm, and BPDU guard with spanning tree shuts any edge port that starts behaving like a switch, preventing a repeat. Rebooting brings the loop straight back, bigger links just fill faster, and a firewall never sees traffic inside one broadcast domain.

ns-0199.why: Securing network components includes their availability: redundant hardware, support contracts and a tested failover runbook. Moving traffic to the standby core keeps settlement running while the vendor replaces the part under contract. Running on a single hot supply risks an unplanned outage, an unapproved lab part bypasses change control, and a voluntary shutdown creates the outage you are trying to avoid.

ns-0200.why: TFTP has no authentication and no encryption, so switch configurations, which often hold credentials and community strings, cross the WAN readable and alterable by anyone on the path. SCP or SFTP gives an authenticated, encrypted channel. A private lease is not encryption, quiet hours do not stop capture, and renaming files is obscurity rather than protection.

ns-0201.why: Controls at higher layers do nothing if someone can reach the cable itself: physical-layer protection means locked conduit to deter tapping, with link encryption so a successful tap yields nothing readable. VLAN tags are just labels in cleartext frames, port security watches MAC addresses rather than light on a fibre, and a clear label only helps an attacker find the run.

ns-0202.why: An undocumented any-any rule defeats least privilege, but deleting it blind can break a process nobody remembers. Reviewing the logs to see what actually uses it, finding an owner, and then replacing it with specific rules through change control closes the hole safely. Leaving it tolerates known risk, and moving it to the top makes it match everything first.

ns-0203.why: A shared key cannot tell devices apart or be revoked for just one of them. Enterprise mode with 802.1X authenticates each device individually, and EAP-TLS uses certificates, so there is no password to print on a card and a lost scanner is revoked alone. Monthly rotation still circulates one secret, MAC addresses are easily spoofed, and a VLAN limits reach without fixing authentication.

ns-0204.why: An extranet gives named outside partners authenticated access to specific services in a segment separate from the internal network. VPN accounts onto the internal LAN hand partners far more reach than tracking needs, a public database exposes shipment data to everyone, and nightly exports are stale and leave full copies in inboxes Tessaly does not control.

ns-0205.why: End-of-support hardware is a lifecycle risk the owner must knowingly accept for a set period, with compensating controls: locking management access to an admin network and logging it reduces exposure until replacement. Doing nothing leaves unowned risk, unofficial firmware adds an untrusted supply chain into the core, and taking depots offline is a disproportionate business impact for a manageable risk.

ns-0206.why: SNMPv2c sends its community string in cleartext and offers no real authentication, so a longer string is just as sniffable. SNMPv3 in its auth-and-privacy mode gives per-user authentication and encrypted traffic, which keeps both monitoring and device configurations safe. Dropping only write access still leaks configuration data, and ending monitoring trades a confidentiality gap for blindness.

ns-0207.why: Frames sent to the all-ones MAC address reach every host in the broadcast domain, so one huge layer-2 segment makes every device process every sensor's chatter. Smaller VLANs bound each broadcast domain, and routing between them adds a point of control between sensors and scanners. Faster switches still deliver every broadcast everywhere, and moving sensors beside servers widens exposure.

ns-0208.why: Copper twisted pair is rated to about 100 metres per segment and picks up electromagnetic interference from heavy power feeds, so this run would be unreliable and could expose signals. Fibre carries light, is immune to that interference and covers the distance easily. A second copper cable duplicates the same flaws, and coiled slack does not shorten the electrical run.

ns-0209.why: Deprecated protocol versions have known weaknesses, so the secure channel should require current versions by design. Where a legacy device cannot comply, isolating it in a restricted segment is a compensating control until it is replaced. Keeping 1.0 everywhere weakens every client for the sake of a few, dropping TLS removes protection altogether, and an overnight cutoff halts depot work.

ns-0210.why: Plain IMAP sends usernames, passwords and mail in cleartext over whatever network the phone sits on. IMAP over TLS on 993 encrypts the whole session, and closing 143 at the edge makes the secure path the only one. Advice to users is not enforcement, a non-standard port is obscurity, and POP3 without TLS has exactly the same cleartext problem.

ns-0211.why: An application-level proxy firewall understands HTTP and TLS connection requests, so it can enforce which destinations servers may reach and log each request; servers that only talk to named update and partner domains leave malware with nowhere to call home. Antivirus alone misses new tools, blocking two ports pushes traffic elsewhere, and capturing everything records the breach rather than preventing it.

ns-0212.why: Endpoint security matters most where the network cannot protect the device. An always-on host firewall with the strictest profile on untrusted networks blocks inbound attacks from other hotel guests.
