Relying on the VPN leaves the laptop exposed before the tunnel is up, enabling protection only in the office inverts the risk, and optional steps for users are routinely skipped.

ns-0213.why: iSCSI is a converged protocol that carries block storage over IP, and it trusts its network heavily: anyone on the segment can sniff or attempt to mount volumes. A dedicated storage VLAN with CHAP authentication keeps users off the path. Database logins do nothing at the block layer, QoS manages priority rather than access, and guest Wi-Fi is the least trusted network available.

ns-0214.why: In tunnel mode, ESP encrypts the entire original packet, including its internal addresses, and wraps it in a new header between the two gateways, which is the standard design for site-to-site links. AH gives integrity with no confidentiality, transport mode leaves the original header readable, and GRE encapsulates without any encryption at all.

ns-0215.why: An IPS that blocks legitimate payment traffic is a self-inflicted outage. Running in detection mode first gives a baseline to tune false positives, then blocking can be enabled with confidence. Blocking everything on day one risks halting settlement, permanent detect-only discards the prevention you bought, and a device fed from a span port sees copies of traffic, so it cannot block inline.

ns-0216.why: A CDN only protects an origin that cannot be reached around it. Restricting the origin to the CDN's address ranges, or an authenticated origin connection, forces every request through the edge's filtering and DDoS absorption, while TLS protects the hop behind it. An unpublished address is easily discovered, a second CDN adds another path, and dropping TLS exposes the back leg.

ns-0217.why: Sniffing is a legitimate diagnostic tool when it is authorised, minimised and protected. Filtering to the application's hosts and a short window captures what the team needs, and handling the file as sensitive data respects the payroll and card data it may contain. Capturing everything for a month over-collects, a shared drive leaks it, and a blanket refusal blocks a legitimate operational need.

ns-0218.why: Radio is a transmission medium anyone in range can receive, and a directional beam still spills well beyond the far antenna. Strong link encryption keeps intercepted frames unreadable, and mutual certificate authentication stops a rogue device posing as either end. Beam width and hidden names are obscurity, and owning both buildings says nothing about who owns the road between them.

ns-0219.why: Micro-segmentation enforces policy between individual workloads, so a compromised web server can reach only the application tier on the ports it needs and never the database directly. That contains lateral movement inside the data centre. An edge firewall does nothing once an attacker is inside, merging tiers removes separation entirely, and an annual review leaves the flat network in place.

ns-0220.why: Certificate-based client authentication ties access to a device Tessaly issued and manages, so a stolen password alone no longer opens the most powerful system on the network. Mutual TLS also authenticates the API to the client. Frequent password changes still leave a single phishable factor, a new port is obscurity, and logging records misuse rather than preventing it.

ns-0221.why: TLS inspection restores visibility into encrypted threats, but decrypting employees' banking and health sessions carries legal and privacy obligations. Category exemptions agreed with Legal and HR, plus notice to staff, keep the control proportionate and defensible. Inspecting everything by default risks a privacy breach, a blanket refusal forfeits the visibility, and silent deployment undermines trust and possibly the law.

ns-0222.why: Guest wireless should be a separate zone that reaches the internet and nothing internal, with client isolation so guests cannot attack each other either. That keeps untrusted devices off meeting-room systems entirely. Weekly passwords still land guests on the internal subnet, a hidden network is easily found, and handing out the staff password puts visitors on the corporate network.

ns-0223.why: Plain RTP can be captured and replayed as audio by anyone on the path, which would expose spoken card numbers. The Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol encrypts and authenticates the media stream, and TLS protects the signalling that carries its keys. A voice VLAN helps quality and separation but does not encrypt, and the internal LAN is exactly where an intruder would listen.

ns-0224.why: Network components should enter service already hardened: default credentials replaced, unused ports shut, and unneeded services disabled, applied from a secure baseline so every unit matches. Later is where hardening gets forgotten, sitting behind a firewall does nothing against an insider or a compromised depot device, and hardening one unit leaves thirty-nine others on factory defaults.

ns-0225.why: Zero trust network access replaces broad network-level trust with per-application access decided each session on who the user is and whether their device is healthy, so a contractor reaches only the apps their work needs. Password rotation keeps the same wide reach, a separate VPN into the same network changes nothing, and banning remote work solves the risk by removing the business function.

ns-0226.why: Split tunnelling trades visibility for performance, so the design should decide the exception rather than the laptop. Sending only named, trusted meeting services direct keeps corporate and general web traffic inside the tunnel, under Tessaly's inspection. Full split tunnelling bypasses egress controls for most traffic, dropping the VPN removes the protected channel, and cameras off dodges the business need.

ns-0227.why: Multiprotocol Label Switching separates customers by labels inside the carrier's network; it provides traffic engineering and isolation, not confidentiality. Traffic still crosses equipment Tessaly does not control, so encryption over the MPLS WAN keeps protection end to end. Dropping IPsec trusts the carrier with everything, rejecting MPLS discards real benefits, and encrypting one system leaves the rest in clear.

ns-0228.why: In software-defined networking the control plane is centralised, so whoever controls the controller controls the whole network. It belongs on an isolated management network, with authenticated and authorised APIs and a redundant standby so it is not a single point of failure. Broad API reach widens the attack surface, and abandoning SDN discards its central policy benefits.

ns-0229.why: AH signs the outer IP header, so Network Address Translation rewriting that header breaks the integrity check every time. ESP with NAT traversal wraps the packets in UDP so they survive translation, and it also gives confidentiality that AH never provided. Asking the carrier to stop NAT is not in Tessaly's control, GRE carries no encryption, and switching off integrity guts the protocol.

ns-0230.why: A volumetric DDoS saturates the internet link itself, so anything behind that link, however powerful, never gets the chance to help. An upstream scrubbing service or the ISP's mitigation absorbs the flood before it reaches Tessaly's pipe. A bigger firewall sits on the far side of the bottleneck, rotating addresses breaks partners, and accepting outages on payments is a business call Finance would not make.

ns-0231.why: A screened subnet holds internet-facing systems in their own zone, filtered from the internet on one side and from the internal network on the other. If the web server is compromised, the attacker still faces a second boundary before reaching the database. Port-forwarding into the LAN puts the attacker inside, no filtering at all invites compromise, and co-hosting erases separation.

ns-0232.why: Sender Policy Framework lists the servers allowed to send for the domain, DKIM signs messages so receivers can verify them, and a DMARC policy tells receivers to reject mail that fails both. Together they let customers' mail systems discard the spoofed invoices automatically. Phone checks shift the burden to customers, a new domain can be spoofed just as easily, and a footer appears on the fakes too.

ns-0233.why: A network sensor can only judge traffic it can read and that passes it. Outside the TLS terminator it sees mostly encrypted sessions, and with none internally it misses east-west movement. Sensors behind the decryption point and on links between zones see the traffic that matters. Per-port sensors are costly noise, and endpoint agents miss unmanaged devices.

ns-0234.why: Cellular links are just another untrusted network. A private access point name from the carrier, or a tunnel back to Tessaly, keeps truck routers off the public internet so there is no exposed admin page to attack. A new password leaves the interface open to brute force and exploits, dropping it from the scan hides the finding, and power schedules still expose trucks on the road.

ns-0235.why: A third-party connection needs both a governance and a technical boundary. An interconnection security agreement sets responsibilities, notification duties and permitted use, and filtering the tunnel to the named hosts and ports enforces least privilege. Any-to-any tends to stay forever, an internal account over-grants, and an obscure public share protects customs files with nothing but secrecy.

ns-0236.why: ICMP is IP protocol number 1, and parts of it are needed: path MTU discovery depends on fragmentation-needed messages, and blocking them causes exactly the stalled large transfers the web team describes. Allowing the essential types while rate-limiting or filtering echo balances reconnaissance risk against function. Blocking everything breaks the network, allowing everything exposes it, and a weekday schedule is not a security design.

ns-0237.why: Auto-negotiating trunks let a device on a user port become a trunk, and a native VLAN shared with users enables double-tagging, both routes to VLAN hopping. Hard-setting user ports to access mode and moving the native VLAN to an unused ID closes both. VLAN separation is only as good as that configuration, crowding users onto VLAN 1 worsens it, and separate hardware is overkill for a configuration fix.

ns-0238.why: A jump host gives one hardened, monitored entry point into the management plane: it enforces multi-factor authentication, keeps a record of every session, and lets router ACLs trust a single source. Direct access from many laptops multiplies entry points, a shared account destroys individual accountability, and exposing SSH to the internet invites brute force against the core.

ns-0239.why: Bluebugging abuses weak or unpatched Bluetooth stacks to take control of a phone, and discoverable devices are easy to find and target. Turning off discoverability after pairing, requiring secure pairing modes and patching the stack remove the entry points while the scanners keep working. Short range is no barrier with directional antennas, a cable-only ban cripples depot work, and random names are obscurity.

ns-0240.why: A protective DNS resolver refuses to resolve known-malicious and newly registered risky domains for every device at once, which breaks many phishing and command-and-control chains before a connection is made, and it logs the attempts. Printed lists age instantly, blocking years of registrations breaks legitimate sites, and public resolvers remove both filtering and Tessaly's visibility.

ns-0241.why: Returned hardware is a data-leaving-the-building event. Sanitising the device, or keeping its storage under a keep-your-media option, protects the ruleset and keys, and rotating any secret it held removes the residual risk if the wipe fails. A confidentiality clause does not stop loss in transit or in a repair depot, partial removal leaves the VPN keys, and tape is not sanitisation.

ns-0242.why: Redundancy that has never been exercised is an assumption, not a control. A planned failover in a change window, with rollback ready, proves that state sync and routing work while limiting impact if they do not. Vendor sign-off at install says nothing about eight months of config drift, an unannounced daytime pull risks a real outage, and rewording the report hides the gap instead of closing it.

ns-0243.why: Virtual eXtensible LAN wraps layer-2 frames in UDP, typically on port 4789, but it has no encryption or authentication of its own: across the internet anyone could read or inject frames into the stretched segment. Carrying it inside an IPsec underlay and filtering its port at the edge keeps the overlay private. Encapsulation is not protection, a spanned flat VLAN is worse, and monitoring only watches the exposure.

ns-0244.why: Network components are only useful as evidence if their logs survive the device and share a timeline. Central collection protects logs from local tampering and loss, and synchronised time via NTP lets events correlate across firewall, switch and VPN. Bigger local buffers still die with the device, screenshots are incomplete and hard to defend, and hand-adjusted timestamps undermine the evidence.

ns-0245.why: Live wall ports in public areas hand any visitor a connection to the internal network. Administratively disabling unused jacks, and activating them only through an approved request, removes that exposure at the transmission medium itself. Receptionists get busy, furniture is moved in seconds, and a label deters only people who were never going to plug in anyway.

ns-0246.why: Remote Desktop exposed to the internet is a favourite ransomware entry point. Closing it and routing the vendor through a remote access gateway or VPN with multi-factor authentication, ideally approved per session and logged, keeps support possible over a controlled channel. Rotating a password still leaves the service open to exploits, a high port is obscurity, and time windows leave it exposed for hours.

ns-0247.why: Egress filtering in line with BCP 38 drops any packet leaving with a source address Tessaly does not own, so a compromised host cannot join spoofed floods or reflection attacks from inside. Blocking the reporter is backwards, denying the report ignores Tessaly's duty of care as an internet citizen, and rate-limiting one uplink leaves every other site able to spoof.

ns-0248.why: Federated identity makes Tessaly's IdP the source of truth: CargoLink trusts signed assertions, so disabling the account at home ends partner access at once and no partner password is left to forget. A monthly list keeps the gap open for weeks; syncing hashes spreads credentials to a third party; a shared login ends accountability.

ns-0249.why: Attribute-driven provisioning ties access to authoritative HR data: when the site or job-code attribute changes, the rules move the person's entitlements with it, closing the mover gap. Manager emails are the manual process that already failed; a quarterly wipe disrupts work and still lags; a second directory adds another source of truth instead of fixing the process.

ns-0250.why: Identity proofing binds a claimed identity to a real person before any credential is issued; checking a government photo ID such as a driver's licence against the HR record does that. A start date and employee number are facts a social engineer can research, and enrolling first, even temporarily, hands an attacker a working authenticator mid-campaign.

ns-0251.why: Disabling contains the misuse, and reissuing the account with only write rights to the export share applies least privilege, so if it is stolen again the blast radius is one folder. A rotation leaves domain-wide privilege in place; deleting destroys evidence and breaks a business process; watching lets someone holding domain admin keep moving.

ns-0252.why: Biometric authentication can be spoofed with a lifted print, so a characteristic alone is weak at a high-value door. Adding the badge makes entry multifactor tonight, and liveness detection targets the spoof itself. Re-enrolling fails because the copy is of the cashier's real finger; lowering sensitivity raises false acceptance, the very failure being exploited.

ns-0253.why: Two reads far apart mean the RFID credential was cloned: low-frequency proximity cards send a static ID any cheap reader can copy. Revoking the ID kills every copy, and a PIN adds a factor the clone lacks. Encrypted cards are the right long-term fix but leave the door open tonight, and recovering the original badge does nothing about the copy.

ns-0254.why: Sessions with no IdP sign-in mean someone is forging assertions with the stolen token-signing key, and every relying party trusts them. Replacing the key and pushing new metadata removes that trust; revoking sessions evicts the attacker. Password resets fail because forged assertions never touch passwords; local accounts scatter credentials and outlast the incident; addresses are trivially changed.

ns-0255.why: Deprovisioning is timed to the termination, and for a hostile leaver with admin rights that means now: disabling accounts, ending sessions and revoking tokens closes every path, and the log shows due care. Waiting for paperwork leaves a live admin session in angry hands; a password change alone leaves open sessions and refresh tokens working.

ns-0256.why: Security questions are a knowledge factor, and knowledge that is public is no longer secret. Adding more of the same factor, or tightening its format, only adds more researchable facts. Replacing it with something the user has, a code on a registered device, stops the resets tonight; tidying profiles helps later but not with answers already exposed.

ns-0257.why: Replication rights let an account ask a domain controller for every password hash, so only domain controllers should hold them. Removing the grant and isolating the host contains it, and treating the hashes as stolen drives resets, krbtgt included. Rebooting drops one session but keeps the right; a password reset leaves the over-privileged grant for the attacker to reuse.

ns-0258.why: Tickets the KDC never issued, with impossible lifetimes, are forged with the stolen krbtgt key. Kerberos honours any ticket signed by that key, so the key must change, twice, because the previous key is still accepted. Lifetime policy fails because forged tickets ignore it; restarts clear memory but the attacker can mint more.

ns-0259.why: The harm is to confidentiality: cardholder data is being disclosed to someone with no need to know. Stopping the person, suspending the over-scoped badge and locking the screens ends the exposure. Deleting the photos destroys evidence, and guards may lack authority to search a phone; powering off loses volatile data and leaves the person in the room.

ns-0260.why: This is a consent grant: the third party holds delegated OAuth tokens, not passwords, so resets and MFA do nothing to access already granted. Revoking the consent and tokens and blocking the app ends it; requiring admin approval for third-party apps stops the next one. Refresh tokens can live for weeks, so waiting leaves mail flowing out.

ns-0261.why: An orphaned account is a lifecycle failure: access outlived the relationship because deprovisioning hung on a ticket nobody raised. Disabling contains it while keeping evidence, and reconciling against the agency's list finds the others. Deleting destroys the identifiers and audit trail an investigation needs; emailing a new password to a third party hands out a fresh credential.

ns-0262.why: A Type 3 factor, something you are, is bound to the body and cannot be lent the way a badge (Type 2) or PIN (Type 1) can, so it restores individual accountability at the door. A personal PIN is still shareable; two badges are the same factor type twice; a logbook relies on a guard and a signature, both easily defeated.

ns-0263.why: Authorization should fail closed: implicit deny with explicit allows means a new group or account gets nothing until someone decides it should. A block list fails open, so every group created tomorrow can call the pricing API. Logging detects misuse after the fact instead of preventing it, and one more blocked group keeps the same flawed model.

ns-0264.why: An identity governance system turns reviews into tracked certification campaigns: data owners attest to real entitlements, evidence is kept, and access nobody certifies is removed instead of left in place. Comments add effort, not assurance; the identity team cannot judge business need, which is the owner's call; reviewing less often lets privilege creep run longer.

ns-0265.why: NIST SP 800-63B favours long passwords checked against known-breached lists, changed only on evidence of compromise. Forced rotation and composition rules breed predictable patterns like seasonal variants, which is exactly what the help desk sees. Faster rotation and stricter composition make the patterns worse, and a difference rule is met by changing the year and symbol.

ns-0266.why: Authenticating the device as well as the person belongs in the identity strategy: MDM enrolment gives each phone an identity the access policy can check, enforces encryption and screen lock, and allows remote wipe when one goes missing. A signed promise is not enforcement; a shared login destroys accountability; an app password does nothing for data cached on an unencrypted phone.

ns-0267.why: Rule-based access control applies the same conditions, source and time, to every subject regardless of identity, which is what 'whoever the user is' requires; it layers under roles, not instead of them. A role alone grants access at any hour from anywhere; owner-set permissions are discretionary and spread access; a reminder is guidance, not a control.

ns-0268.why: Tailgating defeats the reader because it authenticates one person and admits many. A mantrap admits one person per badge read, and anti-passback stops a badge being handed back out for reuse. Signs rely on goodwill that is already failing; exit readers and extra cameras record the problem without preventing it, detection bought in place of access control.

ns-0269.why: In federation the service provider trusts the IdP only through the signature on each assertion. If it accepts edited or unsigned ones, anyone can claim to be anyone and MFA is bypassed because the IdP never sees them. Signature and audience checks are go-live criteria. Shipping now accepts a known total bypass; local passwords abandon federation instead of fixing the relying party.

ns-0270.why: Role-based provisioning gives each joiner the entitlement set defined for the job and agreed with its owner, so access matches function on day one. 'Same as' copying clones nine years of accumulated rights, and the newest agent may carry oddities of their own. Trimming later leaves the excess live meanwhile; listing every system from scratch is slow and error-prone.

ns-0271.why: TACACS+ centralises authentication, authorization and accounting for device administration: each engineer uses their own directory identity, commands can be authorized one by one, and accounting records who ran what. Scripted local accounts sprawl across 300 boxes; a stronger shared password still leaves nobody accountable; RADIUS with one shared account keeps the anonymity the ticket is meant to end.

ns-0272.why: Services need identities too: a distinct workload identity with short-lived, automatically issued credentials lets the shipping API know which service is calling, scope it, and revoke it without breaking four others. A shared key gives no attribution and one stolen copy works everywhere; moving or lengthening it keeps the sharing; an allow list trusts a whole subnet.

ns-0273.why: Just-in-time access removes standing privilege: rights exist only for the approved, time-boxed window when someone needs them, so a stolen engineer account is not an Owner account most of the time. Reviewing logs finds misuse afterwards; two permanent Owners still leave standing privilege and a bottleneck; an admin device helps but does not shrink the time privilege exists.

ns-0274.why: Visitor access is identified, time-limited and supervised: pre-booking ties the visit to a sponsor, an ID check proves who arrived, a dated badge marks them as a visitor, and escorts keep them out of areas they have no reason to be in. A tablet digitises the weak log; permanent badges grant standing access to non-staff; liability transfers cost, not risk.

ns-0275.why: Transitive trust means Tessaly would also trust whoever Harbourline trusts, including the breached subsidiary. A one-way, non-transitive trust with selective authentication admits only Harbourline's users, and only to the named app, so trust stops at the partner. Turning SID filtering off invites privilege escalation across the boundary, and any transitive option inherits the subsidiary's risk.

ns-0276.why: The lifecycle covers more than joiners and leavers: extended absence is a state change, and suspending a dormant high-privilege login stops it being abused unnoticed. Deleting loses history and forces a full rebuild; leaving it active gives an attacker a quiet target; cover for her approvals should be a separate, approved grant to the deputy, not a copy of her rights.

ns-0277.why: Any domain user can request a service ticket, and part of it is encrypted with the service account's password, so a short password falls to offline cracking. Managed service accounts use long random secrets that rotate automatically, leaving nothing worth cracking. Lockouts do not stop a normal-looking request; NTLM is weaker still; a new eight-character password falls the same way.

ns-0278.why: Authorization belongs in the web application's server logic: every request for an object is checked against the signed-in user's rights, which fixes this insecure direct object reference. Hiding the number or moving it to a form field is obscurity any proxy defeats; random identifiers slow guessing but leaked links still work; alerting only detects abuse after invoices leak.

ns-0279.why: A lost master key compromises every lock it opens, so physical access control means rekeying, prioritised by what each door protects, with a guard on the highest-risk store until it is done. Waiting or deferring to a refresh leaves the drug store open to whoever holds the ring; a spare ring restores convenience while doubling the keys in circulation.

ns-0280.why: Bringing the SaaS under central identity and access management means one identity per person: SSO through the corporate IdP applies Tessaly's authentication and MFA, and automated provisioning such as SCIM creates and removes accounts as people join and leave. Quarterly lists leave leavers active for months; blocking punishes the business; a shared login destroys accountability.

ns-0281.why: Privilege creep is access that piles up as people move and nobody removes the old grants. Confirming the current role with the manager and removing what no longer matches restores least privilege; any cover should be a separate, time-bound request. Wiping everything stops her real work tonight, and deferring to an audit leaves excess rights live for months.

ns-0282.why: A biometric threshold trades false rejections against false acceptances. For attendance, a false accept costs little while false rejects stall a shift, so lowering the matching threshold is the right risk call; the same move would be wrong on a high-security door. Raising it lengthens the queues, a second scan doubles the chances of rejection, and iris readers are costly overkill.

ns-0283.why: Mandatory access control is enforced by the system: security sets labels and clearances, and users, owners included, cannot pass access on, which is what the contract demands. Discretionary models let owners grant access, so a rule not to share is only a request; roles without labels ignore clearance; a DLP alert fires after the file has already moved.

ns-0284.why: Non-human identities need a lifecycle too: every account has an accountable owner and documented purpose, and one nobody claims is disabled first, then removed after a quiet period, so a hidden dependency surfaces without an outage. Deleting outright can break a payment job at 03:00; one shared password is worse than the old ones; excluding them from reviews is how this happened.

ns-0285.why: Push fatigue works because a plain approve button needs no context. Number matching makes the user enter the number shown on the sign-in screen, so a prompt they did not start cannot be approved blindly, and location adds a cue. Reminders already failed; a cap still allows bombing; SMS codes are exposed to SIM swap and real-time phishing.

ns-0286.why: Attribute-based access control evaluates attributes of the user, the resource and the context, here region, shift time and device compliance, in one policy at request time, avoiding role explosion. Two hundred groups become unmanageable and drift; one broad role breaks least privilege across regions; case-by-case grants by team leaders are discretionary and leave no consistent rule.

ns-0287.why: Temporary access should be provisioned with its end built in: named accounts keep accountability, a finance sponsor owns the need, and an expiry date removes access without anyone having to remember, which is what failed last year. A shared login loses attribution; full finance rights exceed a read need; old accounts carry unknown history and may belong to people who left.

ns-0288.why: Simple bind sends credentials in clear text; protecting the channel with LDAPS or StartTLS encrypts the bind, and the password already seen on the wire must be treated as exposed and rotated. A VLAN narrows who can sniff but anyone on it still can; faster rotation leaves each new password readable; anonymous bind removes authentication and opens the directory to anyone.

ns-0289.why: Editing supplier bank details and releasing payments are a toxic combination: one person could point a supplier at their own account and pay it. Separation of duties keeps the two in different hands whatever a manager approves. Quarterly sampling finds fraud after the money has gone, and a time limit still leaves a week when one person holds both halves.

ns-0290.why: A rehire is a joiner: access is granted for the new role, not restored from the old one. Reusing the identity is fine, but the stale supervisor groups must go before sign-in is enabled, or she returns with rights she no longer needs. Handing the trim to a manager invites privilege creep, and a second enabled account doubles the attack surface for one person.

ns-0291.why: Kerberos timestamps its authenticators and rejects any outside a small skew, five minutes by default, to block replay. A consistent time hierarchy keeps controllers and servers in step so sign-ins work and logs line up. Hand-set clocks drift beyond tolerance; manual checks miss it between visits; widening tolerance to an hour opens a long replay window.

ns-0292.why: Role-based access control assigns permissions to job-function roles and people to roles, so a new mechanic gets the mechanic role in one step and 'who can edit routes' is answered by looking at one role. A single broad set breaks least privilege; manager-edited permissions are discretionary and drift; a yearly spreadsheet documents the mess without controlling it.

ns-0293.why: A real-time relay forwards whatever code the victim types, so SMS, app and email codes all fall to it. FIDO2 security keys sign a challenge bound to the genuine site's origin, so a look-alike page gets nothing usable: they are phishing-resistant. Longer passwords do not help when the password is captured along with the code.

ns-0294.why: Clearance says what someone may see in principle; need-to-know limits it to what their current work requires. Granting the 12 accounts in her case, and more as cases open, keeps exposure proportionate. Blanket access, even for a month, exposes every customer's history through one account; relaying records through a colleague just moves the disclosure and loses the audit trail.

ns-0295.why: This is credential stuffing: pairs leaked elsewhere replayed at scale. Rate limiting and challenges on risky sign-ins slow it, and screening against breached-password lists stops known pairs working, with forced resets for accounts already hit. Three-strike lockouts let the attacker lock out real customers; geo-blocks are dodged with proxies; a general email changes nothing tonight.

ns-0296.why: Discretionary access control lets owners grant access at will, which is how 'Everyone' landed on M&A data. Removing the grant, sharing the single file, and limiting what owners may grant, such as blocking broad groups, keeps owner flexibility without letting one click expose a folder. Taking every folder into IT kills ownership; deleting the contractor leaves 'Everyone' in place.

ns-0297.why: Two-factor authentication needs factors of different types. A password and a PIN are both something you know, so one phishing page or keylogger captures both. Adding something you have, a code from a registered device or hardware token, is genuine 2FA. Changing the PIN often or lengthening the password still leaves a single factor type.

ns-0298.why: Certificate-based sign-in stops a stolen card only once the relying system learns the certificate is revoked. Revoking it and moving to live OCSP checking closes the week-long gap a stale list leaves. A PIN is a small keyspace and can be observed, so hoping the thief lacks it is not a control; a password reset is irrelevant to card sign-in; a new card leaves the old one working.

ns-0299.why: On shared terminals a session that outlives its user breaks accountability: actions land on someone who has walked away. Short idle timeouts end the session, and a fast badge tap keeps re-authentication practical so pickers do not work around it. A shared login removes attribution entirely; longer sessions worsen it; a notice relies on memory at shift pace.

ns-0300.why: Step-up authentication demands fresh, strong proof of identity at the point of a high-risk action, so a stolen or hijacked session cannot release large payments on its own. Shorter sessions shrink the window but a hijacker can still act inside it; a stronger password protects only the morning sign-in; a next-day email detects the loss after the money has left.

ns-0301.why: Retiring a legacy protocol is a change, and change starts with knowing its dependents: NTLM auditing shows which systems still use v1 so each can be upgraded or isolated before enforcement. Blocking blind risks halting depot operations overnight; leaving it on keeps the relay exposure; an allow rule for a whole subnet exempts every host there, not just the scanner.

ns-0302.why: Continuous authentication re-evaluates trust through the session, not only at sign-in: when the location or device behind a token changes, the platform demands fresh proof, so a replayed token fails at once. An eight-hour session still gave the attacker six hours; the password was never used in the replay; a geo-block is dodged by an attacker renting a UK host.

ns-0303.why: Break-glass accounts give a controlled path when normal authorization fails: kept outside the IdP dependency, credentials sealed, use monitored so every sign-in raises an alert and a review. One admin's private account is standing privilege without oversight; no path at all turns an IdP outage into a lockout; a runbook password is readable by anyone holding the runbook.

ns-0304.why: A unique salt per password means identical passwords produce different hashes, so precomputed tables and crack-once-use-everywhere attacks fail; a deliberately slow algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt makes each guess expensive. Encrypting with a key stored beside the data adds little once the server is breached; a second fast hash barely slows cracking; table permissions do not change what a stolen dump reveals.

ns-0305.why: A privileged access management vault holds the root credential so nobody needs to know it: engineers check it out under their own identity, the vault logs who had it and rotates it after use, restoring individual accountability for a shared account. Emailing a new password recreates the leak; a password on a spreadsheet is a thin wrapper; rotating only on leavers leaves every use untraceable.

ns-0306.why: Spraying tries one common password across many accounts, so per-account lockout barely touches it while handing the attacker a way to lock out dispatchers. Throttling by source, banning common passwords and requiring MFA defeat the spray without a denial-of-service lever. Permanent lockout makes that lever worse; removing lockout leaves unlimited guessing watched only by alerts.

ns-0307.why: An integration's authorization is expressed in the scopes its token carries. Granting only the read scope it needs applies least privilege, so a compromised partner key cannot edit orders or issue refunds. An NDA is a contractual control, not a technical limit; trimming later leaves refund rights live through the pilot; lending your own token destroys attribution and hands over everything you hold.

ns-0308.why: Port-based authentication with 802.1X and EAP-TLS authenticates each device by its own certificate, so a leaked shared key admits nothing and a lost scanner is revoked individually. Rotating a shared key still spreads it to everyone; hiding the network name is trivially bypassed; MAC addresses are broadcast in the clear and easily spoofed by the rogue laptop.

ns-0309.why: Unconstrained delegation lets a server impersonate connecting users to any service, so compromising it yields every cached ticket. Constrained delegation limits impersonation to the one SQL service it needs, which is least privilege for delegation. Keeping admins away helps but leaves every other user's ticket reusable; a SQL admin account loses per-user authorization; antivirus does not change what the server is allowed to do.

ns-0310.why: An assessment strategy needs senior management sponsorship: they approve scope and frequency, own the risk, and fund remediation, so results reach someone accountable. Letting a single team commission tests repeats the orphaned-findings failure, a tool changes nothing about ownership, and hiding reports from management defeats the purpose of assurance.

ns-0311.why: Backup verification data must prove recoverability. Durability only says stored bytes will not be lost, and job success only says a job ended; neither shows the data can be restored intact and on time. Collecting restore-test results measures what matters. Leaning on the durability figure is the tempting error that let this failure go unseen.

ns-0312.why: Rules of engagement define stop conditions and contacts for exactly this: when testing harms production, you halt through the agreed channel, involve the system owner, and resume under revised conditions. Carrying on because it was in scope puts the test above the business. Silently blocking the testers leaves them confused and the record incomplete; a rollback guesses at a cause you already know.

ns-0313.why: A scanner's Medium is a generic base severity. Analysing test output means adjusting priority for asset criticality, exposure and live threat, which is what environmental and temporal context is for. Queuing it by label ignores active exploitation; editing the base score falsifies the record instead of documenting the context; closing it skips the risk owner.

ns-0314.why: Auditors get read-only access limited to the agreed scope, and deviations go through the audit liaison and management. Restricting the account contains the exposure while keeping the record. Independence covers auditors' judgement, not unscoped access to personal data. Deleting files destroys evidence of what happened, and domain admin rewards the overreach.

ns-0315.why: A sound assessment strategy defines what data testers may handle. Access controls can be tested with masked or sampled records, so data minimisation lets the test proceed without exposing health data. An NDA does not make the disclosure necessary, encryption protects transit but not the over-collection itself, and cancelling leaves the controls untested.

ns-0316.why: Log data is security process data, and a gap right after a suspicious admin logon may be an attacker impairing defences. Treat it as an incident and restore collection. The green KPI shows why metrics must measure received events, not configured sources. Restarting and closing loses the question of why logs stopped; waiting trusts a metric that is already wrong.

ns-0317.why: A confirmed non-exercise event is a real attack; the exercise's deconfliction channel has done its job, and now the IR plan takes over. Pausing the exercise removes noise and frees the defenders. Logging it for the report lets a real adversary operate for days, testers are not your incident responders, and wiping destroys evidence.

ns-0318.why: Analysing test output means confirming findings before acting on them: banner-based checks often produce false positives on distributions that backport fixes. A quick check of installed packages on a sample shows whether the risk is real. An estate-wide emergency rebuild on an unverified finding causes its own outage; blanket suppression risks false negatives.

ns-0319.why: ITIL-style change management has an emergency change path: act now, record it truthfully, and have the CAB review it afterwards. That is the evidence auditors want to see. Backdating falsifies audit evidence, an integrity failure far worse than the missing ticket. Rolling back reopens the outage to hide a process gap, and leaving it unrecorded breaks the configuration baseline.

ns-0320.why: Test strategy must cover location: you may test only what you are authorised to test, and a third party's infrastructure needs its permission. Cloud and SaaS providers usually set a testing policy or offer attestations instead. Hosting Tessaly data does not make their systems yours to scan; evading or misleading the abuse desk turns an error into unauthorised access.

ns-0321.why: Account-management data exists to surface exactly this, but an active leaver session is now an incident, not a metric. Disabling the account contains it, the logs preserve evidence, and the remaining 30 then go through the deprovisioning fix. Reporting next week leaves the door open; deleting destroys the audit trail; emailing the leaver may tip off whoever holds the credentials.

ns-0322.why: Dynamic testing that writes data belongs in a test environment that mirrors production. Stopping the scan limits the harm, the business owner decides how to hold the bad orders, and rerunning on staging still gives you the results. Finishing the scan multiplies the damage; deleting records directly bypasses the owner and leaves no trace of what happened.

ns-0323.why: Test output can reveal a real compromise, and that stops being a report finding: it goes to incident response at once, with the host preserved. A months-old web shell means a live adversary may still be inside. Waiting for the report gives them a week, and having testers delete it destroys evidence and tips off the attacker.

ns-0324.why: A SOC 2 Type II report gives an auditor's opinion on security controls operating effectively over a period, which is what vendor due diligence needs. A seal or SOC 3 summary is for the public and lacks detail. Type I covers design at a single point in time, not operation over a year, and SOC 1 addresses controls over financial reporting.

ns-0325.why: Assessment strategy needs independence: the people who build and operate a control should not be the ones attesting it works. An independent assessor, internal or third party, can still use the team's knowledge through design notes and interviews. Self-assessment invites blind spots and bias, and a sign-off inside the same chain of command does not fix that.

ns-0326.why: Credentialed scans read installed software and configuration directly, so they find missing patches that unauthenticated scans cannot see. A dedicated, monitored account with only the rights needed keeps the scanner from becoming an attacker's best credential. The outside view has its place but explains the false clean; domain admin over-privileges; an annual test cannot replace monthly coverage.

ns-0327.why: When a finding cannot be fixed yet, exception handling makes the residual risk visible: compensating controls reduce it, the risk owner formally accepts it, and an expiry forces a revisit. Marking it remediated is false reporting. The SOC lead does not own the business risk, and deleting the finding hides exposure from the people who must decide on it.

ns-0328.why: Misuse case testing asks what an abuser would try, so the tests prove that the feature refuses bad input and fraudulent flows as well as handling good ones. Refunds are a classic fraud target. More happy-path cases only confirm what already works, a load test answers a different question, and user acceptance testing is not designed to find abuse.

ns-0329.why: Reporting fits the audience: the board needs findings in business-risk terms, with priorities and remediation owners, so it can decide and fund. The full report stays attached for traceability. An unedited technical report buries the decision, raw CVE lists mean nothing to directors, and a one-line reassurance withholds risk the board is accountable for.

ns-0330.why: Assessment frequency should follow risk: critical, exposed or fast-changing systems are tested more often, and significant changes trigger a retest. That spends effort where loss is likeliest. An equal rota treats payments like a print server, testing only payments leaves the rest unassessed, and a single cram week optimises cost rather than assurance.

ns-0331.why: An audit closes the loop through management's action plan: each finding gets an accountable owner, a concrete action and a date that audit can follow up. 'In hand' with no owner or date is the usual way findings reappear next year. Disputing everything by reflex damages credibility, and silent fixes leave no evidence the risk was treated.

ns-0332.why: Training and awareness data should measure behaviour, not attendance. How often and how fast staff report a simulated phish shows whether the programme changes what people do. Completion and quiz scores measure activity. Counting clicks has value, but naming people publicly punishes them and discourages the reporting you actually want.

ns-0333.why: A detective control is proven by testing it: run the technique in a controlled, authorised way, as breach-and-attack simulation or purple teaming does, and follow the alert from endpoint to SIEM to analyst. Silence is not evidence of either safety or failure. Tuning for noise hides the question, and waiting for a real attacker makes the adversary your test.

ns-0334.why: Coordinated or responsible disclosure gives the vendor time to fix before details go public, protecting other customers without arming attackers first. It also fits the ISC2 ethics duty to protect society. Publishing tonight exposes everyone before a patch exists, keeping quiet leaves other customers at risk indefinitely, and selling it is plainly unethical.

ns-0335.why: Assessment design starts from objectives: what the organisation needs to know, against which requirement, and what counts as a pass. Only then do you choose the method. Booking whatever was named buys an answer to no question, a relabelled scan misleads the director, and a red team is a different tool for a different objective.

ns-0336.why: Audit value rests on independence: a firm auditing its own work has a self-review threat, and the board cannot rely on the result. Pick an auditor with no stake in the design. Familiarity is exactly the conflict, a different partner at the same firm does not remove it, and a memo from the designer is not an audit at all.

ns-0337.why: With source code in hand, code review and static analysis find flaws such as injection, weak cryptography and secrets in code before they reach production, when fixing them is cheapest. A demo proves function, not security. A contractor's attestation is not evidence, and testing next year leaves card data exposed for months.

ns-0338.why: Assessment strategy must cover every location, and in IaaS the shared responsibility model splits the work: Tessaly tests what it configures, such as identities, network rules, images and storage, and relies on the provider's attestations for the rest. Leaving the cloud out ignores the half Tessaly controls. Testing the provider's hypervisors is unauthorised, and an on-premises plan misses cloud-specific risks.

ns-0339.why: A bridge (gap) letter is management's statement that there have been no material changes since the report period ended. It covers the months until the next report, and you still weigh that residual risk. A Type II covers only its stated period. SOC 3 is a general-use summary, and a Type I speaks to design at one date, not operation over the quarter.

ns-0340.why: Fuzz testing feeds large volumes of mutated or malformed input to find crashes and memory-handling bugs that ordinary tests miss. It suits file parsers exactly, and a test environment keeps the crashes harmless. Replaying two known files only checks those two cases, a network scan does not exercise parsing logic, and relying on partners gives up on input validation.

ns-0341.why: To validate a test strategy, check its coverage against reality. Reconciling scanner, CMDB and network data exposes the unknown assets that attackers find first, and brings them into scope. The scanner sees only what it is pointed at. Waiting on the CMDB leaves the gap open, and scanning the same 1,840 more often only deepens coverage you already have.

ns-0342.why: Complementary user entity controls (CUECs) are the customer's share: the vendor's clean opinion assumes Tessaly operates them. Assign owners and keep evidence, or the assurance chain breaks on Tessaly's side. Filing the report ignores that assumption, the vendor cannot review Tessaly's own users on its behalf, and waiting for an auditor is not operating a control.

ns-0343.why: Test coverage analysis asks what was tested, not how much. Tracing each security requirement to its tests shows which requirements were never exercised. Doubling the test count may just repeat the same paths, a lead's assurance is opinion, and counting assertions measures volume rather than coverage of the requirements.

ns-0344.why: Test strategy covers timing and communication: intrusive testing avoids critical business periods, and system owners and the SOC know when it runs so real alerts are not dismissed as the test. Testing the SOC blind is a separate exercise that needs management approval and a trusted agent, not an accident of poor planning. Cancelling gives up assurance that rescheduling keeps.

ns-0345.why: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organisation's controls are excluded from the auditor's opinion, so assurance over the hosting layer must come from that provider's own report. Assuming the vendor's report covers it leaves the data layer unassessed. The auditor cannot simply redraw scope, and a carve-out is common, not disqualifying.

ns-0346.why: Interface testing checks where systems meet: authentication between them, how each handles the other's malformed or unexpected data, and how errors propagate. Integration flaws live there, and component tests cannot see them. Retesting the parts repeats known ground, and a load test on one side answers a different question.

ns-0347.why: Without third-party attestation, a right-to-audit clause gives Tessaly a way to verify the courier's controls, backed by contractual security duties and breach notification. Liability shifts some cost after the fact but gives no assurance beforehand. Addresses are personal data under privacy law, and paying more does not by itself produce evidence.

ns-0348.why: Match the tester's starting knowledge and access to the threat you want to model. An insider scenario calls for a grey-box test with that role's account and knowledge. A zero-knowledge external test answers a different question, domain admin grossly overstates the threat, and full white-box detail models someone with far more insight than a supervisor.

ns-0349.why: Audit evidence is only reliable if the auditor controls the sample. Provide the complete population and let them select, so the test reflects how the control really operates. Handpicking clean tickets or leaving out late ones misleads the auditor, which is an integrity breach, and an assertion that the process always works is not evidence.

ns-0350.why: Social engineering tests are real attacks on people, so they need written authorisation, agreed rules and a lure that tests judgement without causing genuine harm or eroding trust. Fake bonus cuts can distress staff and trigger employee-relations fallout. Skipping approval removes accountability, and a real executive mailbox blurs the line between test and actual compromise.

ns-0351.why: When a third party needs reliance, a formal security audit is the tool: qualified, independent auditors test controls against defined criteria and issue an opinion others can trust. A self-assessment lacks independence, a scan covers technical flaws rather than the control set, and open browsing by outsiders is neither an audit nor safe.

ns-0352.why: A vulnerability assessment identifies and prioritises known weaknesses across many systems quickly and with low disruption, which is exactly the brief. A penetration test goes deep on exploitation, is slower and riskier, and fits later on the highest-risk findings. Waiting relies on the people who never looked, and connecting unassessed estates imports their risk.

ns-0353.why: Internal audit's value depends on organisational independence: it reports to the audit committee or board so findings about management's systems cannot be softened by that management. Putting it under the CIO creates a conflict of interest that a promise does not remove. Replacing it with SOC self-checks swaps assurance for self-assessment.

ns-0354.why: Physical testers carry a signed authorisation letter with a reachable contact, so a stopped tester can be verified quickly and safely. It protects the testers, the guards and Tessaly. Running from security or police is dangerous, briefing every guard removes what the test is meant to measure, and real badges bypass the controls under test.

ns-0355.why: A nonconformity calls for corrective action: find why the process failed, here the lack of any trigger to reassess after a major change, and fix that with owners and dates, not just the symptom. Updating two assessments corrects the instance but invites recurrence. Appealing on timing or shopping for a new auditor avoids the finding instead of treating it.

ns-0356.why: Scripted synthetic transactions run a known journey on a schedule, so they detect failures even when no real users are present, and they give consistent baselines. Real-user monitoring needs traffic that is not there at night, a pen test looks for security flaws rather than availability, and a survey makes customers your monitoring.

ns-0357.why: Audit evidence must be retained for the period under review and as the retention schedule requires. Deleting it just before an assessment destroys the evidence the auditor needs and looks like concealment. A summary is not the original records, and a personal drive breaks custody and data handling rules.

ns-0358.why: Regression testing confirms a change fixed its target without breaking what already worked. Security features such as session handling are exactly what fixes to authentication code tend to disturb. Testing only the bypass repeats the earlier failure, releasing untested makes production the test, and a quarterly delay leaves a known bypass open.

ns-0359.why: A qualified opinion means some controls did not operate as described. Read the exceptions, judge their impact on the services Tessaly uses, and get remediation or compensating controls before renewal. Treating any report as a pass ignores its content, reports cannot be edited on request, and automatic termination is a risk decision taken without analysis.

ns-0360.why: Compliance checks test systems against an approved baseline automatically and repeatably, for example with SCAP-based content, and they show drift on every server. A yearly spot-check picked by the owners is too thin and too easy to steer, a memo is not a test, and rewriting the baseline skips the question of whether servers meet the current one.

ns-0361.why: Fragile operational technology needs a tailored test approach: passive discovery, gentle, rate-limited scans and an agreed window with the owner, so you gain visibility without stopping the line. Permanent exclusion leaves a blind spot attackers favour. The standard profile is what froze the line before, and the time of day does not change that.

ns-0362.why: A control without evidence cannot be shown to have operated, so the honest answer is that no records exist, followed by a fix: documented, signed reviews from now on. Back-dated minutes or relabelled reviews fabricate audit evidence, breaching the ISC2 code's honesty requirement. Refusing the request obstructs the audit.

ns-0363.why: Testing without written authorisation and agreed rules of engagement is indistinguishable from an attack, legally and operationally. The rules of engagement set scope, windows, permitted techniques, emergency contacts and how captured data is handled and destroyed. Speed is not a control, a verbal promise leaves no record, and predicting findings is not a test plan.

ns-0364.why: Rogue access points are found where they operate: a wireless survey detects every broadcasting AP, and matching it against the approved inventory shows which are unauthorised. A wired scan may miss a bridging device, a questionnaire relies on people admitting it, and a perimeter rule does nothing about an AP bridging inside the network.

ns-0365.why: Testing a log-review control means finding evidence that reviews happened and caught what they should: sample weeks and match admin actions to recorded reviews and follow-ups. An owner's statement is an assertion, not evidence. Logging being on shows the data exists, not that anyone reviews it, and doing the review yourself tests nothing about the control.

ns-0366.why: Scope is part of the authorisation; testing beyond it is unauthorised access, however instructive. The HR data owner must approve a written change first, and the foothold itself is already a finding worth reporting. A verbal nod at 06:00 leaves no record and bypasses the owner, and ending the test punishes testers who did the right thing by asking.

ns-0367.why: A walkthrough shows design; operating effectiveness needs evidence over time. Sample changes across the period and check approval came before implementation. A sound design can still be bypassed in practice, a written assurance from the owner is not independent evidence, and one observed change today says nothing about the other months.

ns-0368.why: A DR test exists to find gaps in the plan, and its output is plan maintenance: correct the stale asset references and step order, then retest to prove the fix. Marking it passed hides a plan that would fail in a real disaster, and buying hardware to match an outdated document fixes the wrong thing.

ns-0369.why: Centralised, tamper-resistant log collection protects log integrity: once events leave the host within seconds, an attacker who clears the local log cannot erase the copy. A bigger local log is still on the compromised box and can still be cleared, and a nightly email leaves a whole day of events exposed before they leave the host.

ns-0370.why: Need-to-know and least privilege say access should match the current job; access kept after a project ends is privilege creep. Pulling the membership stops the exposure while the incident process finds out whether the account or the person is the problem. Letting the copies finish lets the data go, and deleting the share hurts HR while destroying evidence.

ns-0371.why: Human safety is always the first priority; no system, containment step or evidence outranks a life. Evacuate, account for everyone, and let a remote colleague carry on if the work can continue. Staying behind, even with one person, puts people at risk for a task that can be handed off, and silencing a fire alarm endangers the whole building.

ns-0372.why: Detection is followed by triage: validate the event, scope it, and decide whether it is an incident before choosing a response. A signing service talking to an unknown host deserves a fast look at the process, destination and recent changes. Closing on a guess skips the analysis, while a full shutdown or blanket block is a response sized before anyone knows what happened.

ns-0373.why: Recovery must restore to a known-good point, before the compromise began, or the attacker returns with the data. Restoring from before 22:10 and replaying clean transactions balances integrity against data loss. The 00:30 copy almost certainly carries the foothold, and trusting antivirus to clean it gambles on a tool that already missed the intrusion once.

ns-0374.why: A crisis communications plan names who speaks for the organisation and pre-approves how, so statements are accurate, legally reviewed and consistent. An analyst's quick reply can speculate about a breach or contradict legal advice, and silence with no owner lets rumour run. A raw technical timeline may disclose details that help the attacker or prejudice legal notification duties.

ns-0375.why: A hot site is fully equipped and near-current, so it restores service in minutes to hours; it exists precisely for systems whose maximum tolerable downtime is short. A three-hour estimate already breaks the one-hour limit. Waiting to save cost turns a recoverable outage into a business failure, and a cold site takes days to stand up.

ns-0376.why: Least functionality means a system runs only what its role needs; a service that serves no purpose is pure attack surface. Turning it off contains this path, and fixing the build image stops it returning on the next server. A new password leaves the service exposed to its next weakness, and reinstalling from the same default image brings the hole straight back.

ns-0377.why: Patch management scales urgency to risk: an actively exploited flaw on an internet-facing device justifies the emergency change path, with a short sanity test and verification afterwards rather than none at all. Waiting a month leaves a known open door, and patching blind can break remote access for the whole company during an incident.

ns-0378.why: Change management includes an emergency path: urgent changes are made with the minimum authorisation available, recorded, and reviewed retroactively by the board. That keeps the fix fast and the record complete. Waiting for Thursday leaves the attacker connected, and an undocumented rule becomes configuration drift that nobody can explain or safely remove later.

ns-0379.why: Badge anti-counterfeiting features like an embedded hologram exist so guards can spot forgeries; a missing hologram is a red flag that must stop entry. Verifying the visit by calling the vendor on a number Tessaly already holds defeats the social-engineering pretext. An escort still puts a possible impostor beside the servers, and a name on a list does not prove the person is who the badge says.

ns-0380.why: Working with law enforcement is a legal decision: counsel confirms the authority for the request (warrant, subpoena or voluntary consent), what can be released and how custody is documented. Handing the server over without that may breach customer obligations, while a flat refusal harms cooperation. A quick USB copy breaks chain of custody and may be useless as evidence.

ns-0381.why: Media protection covers media in transit: a missing box of customer data is a potential breach, so the incident process starts now and the first question is whether encryption protects the data. That answer drives notification. Waiting a day loses time you may owe regulators, and replacing the tapes fixes the vault while ignoring the data that may be in someone else's hands.

ns-0382.why: Application allowlisting flips the default from allow to deny: only approved software runs, so a never-seen binary is blocked without needing a signature. Finance PCs run a small, stable set of tools, which makes the policy practical. Waiting for signatures leaves the gap open, and blocking one hash fails the moment the attacker recompiles.

ns-0383.why: A parallel test is meant to run the recovery site alongside production without touching live operations; once the test starts harming the business it must stop. Restoring production comes first and the fault becomes a finding. Continuing for timings trades real orders for test data, and turning an accident into a full interruption test risks the outage the plan exists to prevent.

ns-0384.why: Evidence follows the order of volatility: memory, network connections and running processes vanish at power-off, so capture them first, then image the disk. Pulling the plug loses that volatile evidence. Browsing files or running a scan changes timestamps and data on the original, which weakens the evidence if HR or a court later relies on it.

ns-0385.why: A duress signal lets someone under threat ask for help without alerting the attacker; the response is to summon help while keeping up appearances. Asking the guard to confirm out loud could expose him, and going down alone adds a second person to danger. Opening the door gives the intruders what they want.

ns-0386.why: Business continuity keeps critical functions running while systems are recovered; a pre-planned manual workaround is exactly what the BCP is for. Invoking it and briefing people shows why plans need training and exercises. Stopping work turns an IT outage into a business outage, and improvised spreadsheets create uncontrolled copies of stock and customer data.

ns-0387.why: Monitoring must watch the watchers: a critical log source going quiet right after an unusual admin logon matches the attacker technique of impairing defences. The absence of data is itself an indicator. Waiting or treating it as routine gives the attacker free time, and trusting the new host removes exactly the evidence you need.

ns-0388.why: Vulnerability management is risk-based: a medium flaw on an internet-facing payment host can matter more than a critical on an isolated lab box. Weighting severity by exploitability and asset value spends limited effort where the risk is. Scanner order ignores context, and blanket-accepting everything below critical is a risk decision nobody with authority made.

ns-0389.why: A simulation test acts out a realistic disaster scenario, with teams carrying out their recovery steps against it, without disrupting production. It goes further than a walkthrough and stays within the board's constraint. A full interruption test breaks that constraint, a repeated walkthrough learns nothing new, and an emailed plan is a checklist review, the lightest test of all.

ns-0390.why: Differential backups copy everything changed since the last full, so nightly jobs are shorter than a full yet a restore needs only the full plus the latest differential. That meets the four-hour restore target. Incrementals are faster to take but must be applied in sequence, which stretches the restore, and monthly-only backups leave weeks of settlement data unprotected.

ns-0391.why: Configuration management starts with a secure baseline: a documented, approved, hardened configuration applied identically everywhere, which makes drift detectable and patching predictable. Hand setup produces 300 different attack surfaces. Copying a lucky device captures its unknown quirks, and hardening after rollout puts devices on the network with default settings.

ns-0392.why: Media reused outside the original trust boundary must be sanitised to a level that defeats laboratory recovery, such as a verified purge, with the result documented. Deleting files or a quick format only removes directory entries, leaving the data easily recoverable. A label is a handling marking, not a control, and relying on trust hands salary data to a third party.

ns-0393.why: Privileged account management removes standing privilege: credentials are vaulted and checked out just in time, with approval, expiry and session logging, so emergencies are still served. Password rotation alone leaves nineteen always-on targets. A shared login destroys accountability, and giving everyone admin is the opposite of least privilege.

ns-0394.why: Change management applies to planned changes regardless of size: request, impact review, approval, testing, scheduled implementation and a backout plan. A TLS change can break older partner clients, which is exactly what review catches. Small edits made outside the process cause many outages, and filing afterwards turns the ticket into a record instead of a control.

ns-0395.why: Remediation removes the root cause, not just the symptoms: rebuilding hosts cleans up the damage, but the router port that let the worm in is still open. Fixing it across all routers stops reinfection. Closing now invites the same incident, extra antivirus treats the symptom, and watching the router for a month leaves the door open while you wait.

ns-0396.why: Detection tools need ongoing tuning: a precise exclusion for the verified scanning tool removes the false positives while the rule still catches real threats. Alert fatigue is itself a risk, because true alerts get missed. Disabling the rule or excluding the fleet creates blind spots, and more staff to read noise treats the symptom rather than the rule.

ns-0397.why: A DR plan must state who has authority to declare a disaster, backed by named deputies and clear criteria, because failover is costly and hard to reverse. That gives speed with accountability. Letting anyone fail over risks needless disruption, a full board vote is far too slow at 03:00, and leaving it unwritten produces exactly the confusion the plan exists to prevent.

ns-0398.why: A mantrap lets only one authenticated person through at a time, physically preventing tailgating and piggybacking; pairing it with awareness explains why. A reminder email alone rarely changes a polite habit, and new badge readers still let a second person walk through behind the first. Propping the door open removes the control entirely.

ns-0399.why: A legal hold overrides normal retention: once litigation is reasonably expected, relevant records must be preserved for e-discovery, and destroying them can be sanctioned as spoliation. Suspending the purge for the scoped records meets that duty. Letting a routine purge run after notice is still destruction, and an uncontrolled USB copy has no custody record.

ns-0400.why: Log correlation depends on consistent time; synchronising every device to an authoritative source (NTP) and alerting on drift keeps timelines trustworthy across systems. Hand-fixing timestamps fixes one case and invites challenge to the evidence. Monthly manual setting drifts again within days, and SIEM receive time adds variable delays that hide the real order of events.

ns-0401.why: Patch management tests before deployment: a staging trial against the real configuration shows whether the module breaks and gives time to plan a fix or compensating control. Going straight to production risks an outage, and letting customers find the breakage makes them the test. Skipping the patch forever leaves a serious vulnerability without any risk decision.

ns-0402.why: A structured walkthrough (a tabletop review) gathers the people named in the plan to talk through each step, cheaply exposing wrong contacts, missing steps and unclear handoffs before heavier testing. A full interruption or parallel test is premature for a plan nobody has read and costs far more. Waiting for a real outage makes the disaster the test.

ns-0403.why: RAID provides fault tolerance for disk failure, not backup: a deletion, corruption or ransomware attack is written to every disk in the array at once. Only independent backup copies let you restore a prior state. Mirroring has the same limitation, and a snapshot on the same array shares its fate when the array or its controller fails.

ns-0404.why: Configuration monitoring compares devices against the approved baseline; unauthorised drift is both a weakness and a possible sign of compromise, so investigate it, then remediate and enforce the baseline automatically. Rewriting the baseline to match approves unreviewed changes, and ignoring drift lets it grow. New hardware does not fix the process that allowed the drift.

ns-0405.why: A security impact analysis examines how a change alters the system's security posture, here a new file-upload path with new injection and malware risks, so the board decides with full information and the right controls are added. A rollback plan limits outage risk but not a breach. Reviewing after go-live is too late, and a list of developers is not an assessment.

ns-0406.why: After recovery and remediation, the incident lifecycle ends with lessons learned: a review while memories are fresh captures the timeline, what worked, what failed and which controls or processes should change. Closing without it wastes the incident's only benefit. Deleting the notes destroys records you may need for regulators, and waiting for the next incident lets the details fade.

ns-0407.why: An IPS sits inline and can drop malicious traffic; an IDS on a mirror port only sees copies and can only alert. Starting in alert mode lets you tune rules before blocking, so false positives do not take down payments. A mirrored sensor cannot block what it never carries, and a honeypot or turning detection off leaves the segment with no protection at all.

ns-0408.why: Recovery priority should follow the business impact analysis: systems with the shortest maximum tolerable downtime and recovery time objectives come back first. That puts effort where delay causes the most harm. Alphabetical order or ease of restore ignores business impact, and taking requests from whoever shouts loudest turns a plan into a negotiation mid-disaster.

ns-0409.why: Mobile devices will be lost or stolen; full-disk encryption makes the data unreadable without credentials, and remote wipe plus revoking VPN access close the rest. An asset sticker helps inventory, not confidentiality. Hiding advice is a weak habit, and insurance covers the hardware while doing nothing for the payment data on it.

ns-0410.why: Evidence collection must preserve integrity and provenance: sealing the device and keeping a chain-of-custody record of every person who handled it, when and why, lets the evidence stand up later. Taking it home or leaving it on a desk leaves gaps anyone can challenge, and booting it changes data and timestamps on the original.

ns-0411.why: When no patch exists, use a compensating control that reduces exposure: segmenting the vulnerable printers limits who can reach them until the fix is available. Waiting accepts the risk without anyone deciding to, and unplugging halts shipping for a threat you can contain. Home-made firmware voids support and can brick the fleet.

ns-0412.why: A checklist (read-through) test has each team review its part of the plan for accuracy: current contacts, equipment and steps. It is the cheapest way to catch staleness before investing in heavier tests. Parallel or full interruption tests on an unverified plan waste effort and add risk, and skipping tests leaves a plan that may fail when needed.

ns-0413.why: Backups are a ransomware target, so at least one copy must be immutable or offline and out of reach of production credentials, in line with the 3-2-1 approach. More frequent copies to a reachable share are encrypted just as fast, and local restore points are commonly deleted by ransomware. Protecting backups with the same admin account leaves them exposed to the same compromise.

ns-0414.why: Configuration standards give every build the same approved, hardened settings; starting from a recognised benchmark and tailoring it to Tessaly's needs is faster and better tested than inventing one. Individual habits create inconsistent attack surfaces. Writing from scratch duplicates effort and misses known issues, and a pre-hardened model still needs Tessaly's own standard to stay consistent.

ns-0415.why: A sound change request includes a backout plan: tested steps to restore the previous state, the conditions that trigger it and who decides. Without one, a failed change becomes an unplanned outage. Approval does not undo a failure, a morning fix leaves customs filings broken overnight, and warning the service desk plans for failure instead of preventing it.

ns-0416.why: In the incident lifecycle, containment comes before convenience: active exfiltration must be stopped to limit damage, and the business impact of the sync is managed separately. Waiting two and a half hours lets more data leave. Wiping now destroys the evidence needed to understand the breach, and waiting on a hosting provider hands your response to someone else.

ns-0417.why: A honeypot works by enticement, being there to be found, not by entrapment, actively inducing someone to commit an offence they would not otherwise commit. Entrapment can undermine legal action and create liability. Placing the decoy on the real payments network or seeding it with real data turns a research tool into an actual exposure.

ns-0418.why: A cold site provides the building and utilities but no equipment or data, so recovery takes days to weeks. It is the cheapest option and fits a service whose maximum tolerable downtime is two weeks. A hot site overspends on a low-priority system, having no site at all ignores the two-week limit, and payments would badly miss their downtime limits on a cold site.

ns-0419.why: CCTV deters, detects and records, but detection needs someone watching or alerting, and investigation needs recordings retained long enough to be reviewed. Removing cameras loses the deterrent and the evidence. More cameras without monitoring or retention just record more that gets overwritten, and dummy cameras can deter but never detect or record.

ns-0420.why: Evidence processing protects integrity: confirming the hash shows the image has not changed since collection, and working on a copy keeps the original pristine for verification or court. Mounting the original read-write may alter it. Skipping verification leaves integrity unproven, and working on the live server changes evidence and alerts any attacker still inside.

ns-0421.why: Unauthenticated scans see only what is exposed on the network, so they miss outdated software inside the host. Credentialed scans log in and check installed versions and configuration, giving a far more complete picture. Accepting the outside view ignores insiders and attackers who get a foothold, a new scanner has the same blind spot without credentials, and scanning less often is worse.

ns-0422.why: High availability depends on removing single points of failure: redundant servers must not share one rack, power feed or network path. Separating the pair makes one PDU failure survivable. A spare PDU still needs a manual swap during an outage, a third node in the same rack shares the same failure, and removing redundancy makes things worse.
