ns-0423.why: Reciprocal (mutual aid) agreements are cheap but fragile: the partner's capacity changes, the agreement is hard to enforce, and hosting may expose Tessaly's data. A doubled workload means the capacity assumption must be retested, with a contracted alternative if it no longer holds. Relying on good faith ignores the risk, and insurance pays out money but does not keep the business running.

ns-0424.why: Change management recognises standard changes: low-risk, repeatable tasks with a proven procedure are pre-approved once, then carried out and logged without a board review each time. That keeps the record and frees the board for real risk. Dropping it from the process loses the record, and letting each engineer improvise throws away the proven procedure that made it low risk.

ns-0425.why: Incident reporting duties run on legal and contractual timelines that do not wait for a complete investigation; legal determines who must be told, by when and in what form, and notices can be updated as facts emerge. Waiting risks missed deadlines and penalties, notifying without review risks inaccurate statements, and notifying only if the press finds out breaks the obligation itself.

ns-0426.why: A backup is only proven by a successful restore: regular test restores catch corrupt media, missing files and broken procedures before a real loss. A completed job can still hold unusable data. More frequent copies multiply an unverified process, and waiting for a real failure makes the incident the test.

ns-0427.why: Sandboxing runs unknown files in an isolated environment and watches their behaviour, catching malware that signatures miss before it reaches users. Blocking every attachment breaks legitimate invoicing, and asking staff to judge file sizes offers no real protection. Waiting for signatures leaves users exposed to exactly the new threats already getting through.

ns-0428.why: A clipping level sets a baseline threshold of normal errors, so alerts fire only when failures exceed it in a set window, which is what a brute-force attempt looks like. That filters the noise without losing the signal. Turning alerts off hides real attacks, more analysts spend time on typos, and watching only executives ignores the service and admin accounts attackers prefer.

ns-0429.why: Preparation is the first phase of incident response: current roles, authority and 24/7 contacts for technical, legal and communications support must be defined and known before an incident. Hunting for contacts mid-incident wastes the hours that matter most. A new tool does not tell you who to call, and a plan full of departed staff will fail when needed.

ns-0430.why: Acquired services are governed through the contract: a notification deadline, a right to audit and an independent SOC 2 Type II report turn vendor promises into evidence Tessaly can check. Renewing unchanged accepts the same blind spot; a discount compensates without reducing risk; rebuilding in-house is a large decision this lesson alone does not justify.

ns-0431.why: A secrets manager takes credentials out of source entirely, and secret scanning in pre-commit hooks and the pipeline catches the next slip before it spreads. A private repo still exposes keys to every insider and every clone; a reminder is awareness without a control; purging history cleans this one leak but prevents none.

ns-0432.why: Error paths must fail secure: when the check cannot complete, the answer is deny. Hotfixing the catch block closes the open door now; the timeout's root cause is fixed next. Keeping it open trades revenue for fraud exposure nobody accepted; a longer timeout still fails open when it trips; an alert only watches the breach continue.

ns-0433.why: Disposal is an SDLC phase: retiring software means removing the service, its access and its data paths, and keeping the evidence. Shutting it down and revoking its credentials contains the exposure; preserved logs show what was taken. Patching sustains a system nobody owns; IP blocks are easily dodged; waiting on a disbanded team leaves customer data open.

ns-0434.why: Contain first by disabling the abused function, then close the gap: automated scanners find known technical flaw patterns, not business-logic abuse such as repeat redemption, so manual business-logic testing is needed. Rescanning repeats a test blind to this class; banning one account leaves the flaw for the next; writing it off accepts a risk nobody assessed.

ns-0435.why: Open-source components arrive transitively, so only an inventory answers exposure: a software bill of materials and software composition analysis show every direct and nested copy, letting you prioritise mitigation. Asking leads relies on memory that misses transitive use; blocking everything is an outage with no scope; waiting for the patch wastes the hours you need to mitigate.

ns-0436.why: Small, frequently integrated commits keep main shippable, so a fix isolated in its own change can pass the pipeline tonight. The habit of avoiding frequent commits is what built a six-week branch whose merge would drag untested code into production mid-incident. Holding the fix leaves the flaw exploitable; hand-patching creates drift the next deploy overwrites.

ns-0437.why: Stopping the job contains the loss. The root cause is missing referential integrity: a foreign-key constraint makes the database refuse child rows without a valid parent, or cascade the delete. Hand-deleting today's orphans lets the next script create more; ending ID reuse hides the symptom; finishing the run multiplies the payments you must claw back.

ns-0438.why: A documented, reusable release process is what the Capability Maturity Model calls Repeatable: success no longer depends on one person, so the team can reproduce it under pressure. Improvising risks a broken or untraceable build; waiting leaves the exploit open for hours; copying files into production bypasses testing and change control and creates drift.

ns-0439.why: Regression testing re-runs known-fixed cases against every change, so an old bug cannot silently return; making the March exploit a pipeline gate makes the fix permanent. Asking for care is not a control; a quarterly pen test is far too infrequent for weekly changes; a freeze blocks legitimate work and protects only these files.

ns-0440.why: A tampered vendor update is a software supply-chain compromise: contain by isolating what runs it and stopping further updates, and keep the package and runners as evidence. Reinstalling in place destroys evidence and trusts an unverified channel; running on lets a compromised runner poison releases; disclosure goes through coordinated channels once facts are known.

ns-0441.why: API keys are credentials: a leaked one is revoked and reissued, and per-key throttling at the API gateway caps what any key can harvest next time. IP blocks are evaded by rotating addresses while the stolen key keeps working; switching the API off punishes every partner for one leak; waiting for business hours leaves customer data flowing out.

ns-0442.why: Assembly has no type safety, bounds checking or compiler guardrails, so memory bugs hide easily and ordinary tools cannot see them. Secure coding standards call for a reviewer competent in the language, focused on buffers near PIN data. Functional tests say nothing about overflow; a C analyser cannot parse assembly; comments after merge do not make it reviewed.

ns-0443.why: In Agile, security belongs in every iteration: security user stories and definition-of-done criteria are built and tested each sprint while fixes are cheap. A single end review finds six months of flaws when they cost most; forcing waterfall fights the team's delivery model instead of joining it; signing off a self-assessment is no assessment at all.

ns-0444.why: The Common Weakness Enumeration gives every tool's finding one shared name, so duplicates collapse, and the CWE Top 25 points effort at the weakness types most often exploited. File order ignores risk; suppressing by each tool's own label hides what nobody assessed; a fifth tool adds another vocabulary to the same pile.

ns-0445.why: Software configuration management ties every deployed build to a tagged commit and a versioned, stored artifact, so you always know what is running and can rebuild or roll back. Reinstalling the newest fixes today but not the cause; choosing by preference skips any security check; confiscating devices halts operations without fixing untracked builds.

ns-0446.why: Client-side checks are a convenience; an attacker posts straight to the server. Secure coding requires server-side input validation, and an allow-list of what is valid beats trying to block what is bad. A stricter browser check is still bypassed; hiding the field is obscurity; logging records the attack without stopping it.

ns-0447.why: A bottom-up security effort lacks authority and budget, which is why it stalls; a top-down approach, with senior management sponsoring and mandating the standard, gives it force. Publishing without backing produces a document nobody follows; issuing policy yourself exceeds your authority; unpaid out-of-hours work is unsustainable and still unenforced.

ns-0448.why: Sandboxing runs untrusted code in a contained environment, so you can observe what it really does without risking real systems or secrets. Trialling it on a production build server exposes signing keys and pipelines; popularity is not a security assessment; a formatter rewrites source, so it can change exactly what the code does.

ns-0449.why: Every API endpoint must authorise access to each object, not just authenticate the caller; without that, changing the ID reads other customers' orders (broken object-level authorization, top of the OWASP API list). Random IDs slow guessing but leaked IDs still work; undocumented endpoints are found by watching traffic; login proves who called, not what they may read.

ns-0450.why: Parameterized queries keep code and data apart: the database treats input strictly as a value, which defeats SQL injection at its root. Deny-list filters are bypassed with encodings and dialect tricks; a WAF is a useful extra layer but leaves the flaw in the code; HTML encoding protects browsers, not SQL parsers.

ns-0451.why: The spiral model is risk-driven: each loop starts by identifying and resolving the biggest risks before prototyping and building, which suits high-risk work with unclear requirements. Waterfall assumes requirements nobody knows yet; code-and-fix has no planned risk review at all; a vendor's preference is not a decision based on Tessaly's risk.

ns-0452.why: Fuzz testing throws huge volumes of unexpected, malformed input at a program to expose crashes, hangs and memory errors that hand-picked samples never trigger, which is the real risk for a parser facing untrusted uploads. More hand-written samples still test only what the team imagined; a pilot sends friendly input; documentation review executes nothing.

ns-0453.why: Code signing binds each release to Tessaly's key, and verification on the device rejects anything altered or unsigned, whoever can write to the share. Renaming is obscurity; a checksum on the same share is swapped along with the installer; silent installs give staff nothing to notice.

ns-0454.why: Sound exception handling catches the errors you expect, deals with each deliberately and leaves no half-finished transaction, while unexpected ones stop the operation safely. Swallowing everything hides failures and can leave refunds half-applied; removing handling crashes users and may leak internals; console stack traces go unmonitored and risk leaking detail.

ns-0455.why: Initiation is where security is cheapest: establishing data sensitivity and writing security requirements into the charter shapes budget, design and tests from day one. A beta pen test finds requirement gaps when they are costly to fix; waiting for a design means it is built without requirements; a password policy covers one control, not the portal's needs.

ns-0456.why: Code coverage analysis shows how much code the tests actually exercise; a green suite that never runs the lockout and reset paths proves nothing about them, and those paths are prime attack surface. Passing tests are not evidence for untested code; deleting security features games the metric; deferring ships unverified authentication.

ns-0457.why: Separating development, test and production environments, and the people working in each, stops untested changes and unaccountable access reaching production; genuine needs are met with approved, time-bound, logged access. Rights in dev do not justify production; copying live data into dev spreads it to weaker controls; a shared login destroys accountability.

ns-0458.why: Assembly offers no bounds checks or type safety, so a new string parser there invites buffer overflows; secure coding guidance is to put new input-handling logic in a memory-safe language and keep the low-level surface small. One-language consistency is not a security argument; comments do not prevent overflows; forum code adds unknown provenance to the riskiest part.

ns-0459.why: Dynamic application security testing exercises the running application from outside, finding session, header, configuration and runtime flaws static analysis cannot see; authenticating the scan reaches pages behind login. Rerunning SAST repeats the same blind spot; scanning production at peak risks outages and data changes; reading code is not testing its runtime behaviour.

ns-0460.why: Context-aware output encoding makes the browser treat user text as text, not markup, which prevents stored cross-site scripting whatever slipped past input checks. Short payloads still fit in 200 characters; courier accounts can be phished or misused; a weekly scan leaves days of exposure and misses scripts written without script tags.

ns-0461.why: Certification is the technical assessment; accreditation is management's formal decision to operate the system and accept its residual risk, and that authority sits with the accountable owner, not the analyst. Signing yourself exceeds your authority; blocking outright substitutes your risk appetite for the business's; launching quietly hides risk from the people accountable for it.

ns-0462.why: Source code escrow lodges the code with a neutral third party and releases it to Tessaly if the vendor goes under or abandons the product, protecting continuity without taking the vendor's IP. A discount does not keep the software running; outright source transfer is rarely agreed; signing with no plan leaves a critical dependency without an exit.

ns-0463.why: Test environments rarely carry production controls, so live cardholder data there multiplies exposure and breaks data-protection duties; masked or synthetic data with realistic distributions and volume gives valid results. Internal is not the same as safe; restricting access still puts real card data in a weaker environment; refusing tests pushes performance risk into production.

ns-0464.why: Regenerating the session identifier at authentication prevents session fixation, where an attacker plants a known ID before login; Secure and HttpOnly keep the cookie off plain HTTP and away from scripts. A shorter lifetime still lets a fixed ID be hijacked; base64 is encoding, not protection; a CAPTCHA does nothing for the session itself.

ns-0465.why: The DevOps principle of flow favours small batches moving steadily from commit to release; fast automated checks on each change remove the security queue instead of feeding it. Weekly batches only shrink the pile; more reviewers speed up a bottleneck without removing it; scanning after deployment ships the very flaws the scan exists to catch.

ns-0466.why: Interface testing checks the exchanges between components, including malformed, duplicated and out-of-order messages, which is where two individually correct systems fail together. Separate passing suites never exercise the seam; more unit tests stay on either side of it; watching production after release turns the live ledger into the test environment.

ns-0467.why: Secure error handling gives users a generic message and a correlation ID while full detail goes to protected server logs, so support can still trace the fault without handing attackers schema and path details. Staff accounts get phished; an HTML comment is visible in page source; silent reloads confuse users and help nobody diagnose anything.

ns-0468.why: A software assurance maturity model such as OWASP SAMM measures the practices themselves across governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, giving a repeatable baseline and targets to track. One pen test's count reflects its scope and timing more than practice; self-rating is opinion; a scanner score measures one activity through one tool's rules.

ns-0469.why: Acceptance testing is where the business verifies the system meets its requirements, and security requirements belong in that traceability: each gets a test and pass criteria before rollout. The vendor's testing is not Tessaly's acceptance; one scan finds known flaws, not whether encryption and recovery requirements are met; testing after rollout accepts unverified controls.

ns-0470.why: This is a race condition, time of check to time of use. Concurrency control, doing the check and the debit atomically in one locked transaction, makes the second request see the reduced balance. A delay narrows the window without closing it; reconciliation recovers losses after the fact; greying out a button stops honest double-taps, not scripted requests.

ns-0471.why: Cross-site request forgery works because the browser attaches the session cookie automatically; a per-request anti-CSRF token the attacker cannot read, plus SameSite cookies, lets the portal reject forged requests. Switching to GET makes forgery easier; advice to staff is not a control; encryption at rest protects stored data, not the request that changes it.

ns-0472.why: Misuse case testing models what an attacker or abuser would do, such as negative amounts, replayed tips or stolen cards, and checks the feature refuses it. More happy paths still test only intended use; the provider sees card fraud but not negative-tip logic inside Tessaly; letting complaints find abuse turns customers into the test team.

ns-0473.why: Mutation, or dumb, fuzzing needs no specification: it flips bits and alters fields in real samples, so it suits undocumented formats and finds crashes quickly. Generation-based fuzzing needs the spec you may never get; valid files test only normal input; crashes and hangs are meaningful whether or not the format is documented.

ns-0474.why: Static application security testing reads source without running it, so it can gate each pull request and flag injection, crypto misuse and similar flaws minutes after they are written. Twice-yearly pen tests still find them months later; network scanners do not examine application code; unguided reviewer checks are inconsistent at forty merges a day.

ns-0475.why: A fix counts only once verified: retesting each finding against the new version is the evidence that closes it, and anything still exploitable stays open. A vendor email or release note is a claim, not proof; waiting a year leaves genuinely fixed items marked open and hides the true risk picture.

ns-0476.why: Commercial software ships for easy installation, not security, so before go-live Tessaly hardens it to a secure baseline: change default credentials, remove sample content and disable unneeded features to shrink the attack surface. Vendor defaults are not your risk decision; deferring hardening leaves defaults live; a firewall does not fix a known default admin password.

ns-0477.why: Threat modeling at design time, walking data flows and trust boundaries with a method such as STRIDE, surfaces risks like spoofed update servers and tampered packages while design changes are cheap, leading to controls such as signed packages. A pen test after coding finds design flaws at the costliest point; high privilege demands more scrutiny, not less; antivirus misses tailored payloads.

ns-0478.why: Rapid-development prototypes prove an idea; they skip requirements, design review and testing, so they must be rebuilt or brought through the full SDLC before handling real payments data. Hardening after launch exposes real drivers now; removing one known flaw leaves the unknown ones; an unshared URL is obscurity, not access control.

ns-ev-exec-risk.text: 03:45 — The CISO, unable to sleep, messages the desk directly: the board pre-read is due at 08:00 and the annualized-loss figures for the top three scenarios read wrong to her. Sanity-check the exposure math before it goes to print.

ns-ev-execution.text: 03:30 — A spreadsheet on a workstation in accounts payable just spawned a shell, and the shell spawned a script host, and the script host is pulling something down over an encrypted channel. Word documents do not usually have children.

ns-ev-exfil.text: 05:10 — Outbound volume from the file segment is running nine times its nightly norm, chunked into polite parcels and routed through a cloud storage API your business does use — just never at 5 a.m., and never this much.

ns-ev-impact.text: 05:20 — File servers are renaming their contents with an extension you have only seen in incident reports, shadow copies are being deleted in bulk, and a text file titled HOW_TO_RECOVER just appeared in every share. The quiet part of the night is over.

ns-ev-impair.text: 04:10 — Three EDR agents went silent inside two minutes, a log-forwarding pipeline is dropping events on the floor, and someone just tried to add an exclusion path to the on-access scanner. Your eyes are being put out one by one.

ns-ev-initial.text: 03:20 — A finance analyst just entered credentials on a page that looked exactly like your SSO portal, and an inbound VPN session followed forty seconds later from an address no employee has ever used.

ns-ev-lateral.text: 04:40 — The compromised workstation just opened admin sessions on three servers in a segment it should not be able to see, riding remote-service credentials that checked out as valid. The map you failed to defend is being walked.

ns-ev-persistence.text: 03:40 — Change monitoring reports a new scheduled task, a fresh run key, and a service account nobody remembers creating — all in the last hour, all on machines that were clean at midnight. Someone is making sure a reboot will not evict them.

ns-ev-privesc.text: 03:50 — A helpdesk account that has never touched a server just requested a domain-admin token, citing a change window that is not on the calendar. The request is syntactically perfect. That is what worries you.

ns-ev-recon.text: 03:00 — A cluster of week-old lookalike domains is walking your public surface: DNS lookups, careers-page scrapes, a polite portscan that stays just under the alerting threshold. Someone is drawing a map of you.

ns-ev-resource.text: 03:10 — Intel flags fresh infrastructure staged in your name: a typosquatted package on a public registry and a signing certificate bought by a shell company. Nothing has touched you yet. It is being built to.

ns-ev-stealth.text: 04:00 — Nothing is alerting, which is the problem: a review pass shows outbound traffic timed to mimic your backup jobs, binaries named one character off from system utilities, and logons that only ever occur inside business-hours noise. Somebody is dressing as your baseline.

ns-f1-01.why: Controls follow requirements, and a system's security category is set by its highest-impact data, the high-water mark, because attackers go for the bank details, not the FAQs. Averaging or counting volume under-protects the most sensitive data; waiting for an audit leaves it exposed now. Splitting refund data into its own system is the lever if the higher baseline is too costly.

ns-f1-02.why: When a required control cannot be applied, a compensating control meets the requirement's intent another way: forcing access through an MFA-protected, monitored jump host gives equivalent assurance around the console. A long password is still one factor; an exception with no compensation leaves the risk untreated; ripping out production kit this week is disproportionate.

ns-f1-03.why: Scoping removes baseline controls that do not apply to a system's actual components, and recording why keeps the decision auditable. Implementing controls for hardware that is not there wastes effort and muddies evidence; deleting them corporately strips them from laptops that need them; deferring to the auditor abdicates a decision the owner should make.

ns-f1-04.why: Common, or inherited, controls are provided once for many systems by a common control provider such as the data centre; a system inherits them and documents the dependency rather than duplicating them. Parallel physical controls waste money and create conflicts; camera footage is sensitive; picking half the set arbitrarily is neither tailored nor justified.

ns-f1-05.why: Tailoring adjusts a baseline to a system's real risk; here that means supplementing it with dual approval and integrity monitoring aimed at the identified threat. A baseline is a starting point, not a finish line; jumping every family to high spends heavily on risks you do not have; cutting unrelated controls without analysis opens new gaps.

ns-f1-06.why: Natural access control, a CPTED principle, uses the layout itself, such as landscaping, fencing and one obvious route, to steer people where they should go, cheaply and around the clock. Guards are costly and only as good as their attention; signs rely on goodwill; closing the counter breaks the business the depot exists for.

ns-f1-07.why: Natural surveillance, a CPTED principle, puts assets and activity where people can easily see them, with lighting, sightlines and staffed areas, so would-be thieves feel observed and staff notice problems. A hidden corner invites tampering; a sign with no eyes behind it is a bluff; a heavier lock resists but nobody sees the attempt; appointments add friction without need.

ns-f1-08.why: Site selection is the first facility control: natural hazards such as flooding and man-made ones such as flight paths are far cheaper to avoid than to engineer around, and a backup site must survive when the primary does not. Raised racks do not protect power or access; 'only in an emergency' is exactly when it must work; security has to inform the choice, not just cost.

ns-f1-09.why: Territorial reinforcement, a CPTED principle, makes ownership of a space visible through signage, distinct flooring and a reception point, so outsiders know they are entering private territory and staff feel entitled to challenge them. It works now and cheaply. Waiting a year leaves the gap open; hourly patrols miss most drift-ins; challenges work better once the boundary is clear.

ns-f1-10.why: A business continuity plan must be maintained as the organisation changes; new tools and working patterns change recovery steps, dependencies and contacts. Regular reviews triggered by major change keep the plan usable. Leaving it stale means recovery steps no longer match reality, waiting for a disruption makes the plan fail first, and a vendor's generic guide does not reflect Tessaly's processes.

ns-f1-11.why: A tabletop exercise gathers decision-makers to discuss a realistic scenario step by step, testing roles, decisions and communication without touching operations. It reveals gaps in the plan and leaders' understanding cheaply. Closing warehouses or failing over systems is disruptive and aimed at technical recovery, and reading the plan alone does not rehearse any decisions.

ns-f1-12.why: A vital records programme identifies the records the business needs to operate and recover, such as contracts, insurance and legal documents, and keeps protected copies off-site. A single cabinet can be lost in one fire or flood. A scan on the same site's server shares the same risk, and shredding the originals destroys records Tessaly may need to prove its rights.

ns-f1-13.why: Emergency response guidelines give people the immediate actions to protect life and safety: who to call, how to evacuate, what to do first. They must be short, visible and practised. A 90-page plan will not be read in a crisis, leaving it to whoever is senior produces inconsistent responses, and an outside firm cannot act in the first minutes on site.

ns-f1-14.why: A predictable header hands an attacker matching plaintext and ciphertext, the raw material of a known-plaintext attack, and a fixed key with no IV makes identical plaintext encrypt identically. A modern authenticated mode with random IVs and rotated keys resists that. Rewording the header yearly still gives known plaintext; a longer key under the same weak mode keeps the pattern.

ns-f1-15.why: A fault injection attack deliberately disturbs voltage, clock or temperature so hardware misbehaves, for example skipping a security check. Devices with sensors that detect glitches and respond by halting or erasing keys resist it. Glue is a weak barrier anyone with time defeats; betting on low interest ignores unattended depot counters; fraud detection only catches losses afterwards.

ns-f1-16.why: Configuration management scales through automation: tooling applies the approved baseline identically every time and reports devices that fall out of compliance, removing human error. A longer checklist adds more steps to miss. Letting engineers pick settings creates inconsistency, and dropping hardening leaves every laptop at its insecure defaults.

ns-f1-17.why: Configuration management depends on knowing what you have: an accurate, automatically updated asset and configuration inventory (a CMDB) answers exposure questions quickly and underpins patching and incident response. Email surveys are slow and incomplete, ad-hoc scans take time and miss offline systems, and switching vendors still leaves you not knowing where each version runs.

ns-f1-18.why: This is an industry-standards investigation: Tessaly Pay's obligations come from its contracts with the card brands, which can require an approved PCI forensic investigator and impose fines or withdraw processing if ignored. The internal team supports that work rather than replacing it. Lack of statutory authority does not void a contract, no court order is needed, and deleting logs is evidence destruction.

ns-f1-19.why: Physical controls protect the box, not the network path to it: anyone on the office network can reach the console, so the cage does nothing for that route. Logical access controls, named accounts, disabling the default login and restricting which hosts may connect, protect the system where it is actually exposed. More locks or cameras on the cage harden the wrong door.

ns-f1-20.why: Vulnerability management is a cycle, and verification closes it: a follow-up scan confirms each vulnerability is actually gone, catching failed installs, pending reboots and missed hosts. A tool's success report shows the job ran, not that the fix is in place. Patching more often repeats the blind spot, and a new tool without verification has the same gap.

ns-f1-21.why: A parallel test brings the recovery site up and runs real workloads there alongside production, proving it can take the load without interrupting the live service. A full interruption test shuts production down and carries real risk. Walkthroughs and checklist reviews check the plan on paper but do not show the site can process transactions.

ns-f2-01.why: PASTA (attack simulation plus threat analysis, run as a process) is a seven-stage risk-centric method that starts from business objectives and ends with impact and risk analysis, which is exactly what the board wants. STRIDE is useful for categorising threats but produces a technical list, while scans and penetration tests find flaws in built code rather than modelling threats before launch.

ns-f2-02.why: A plausible denial of an action is STRIDE's repudiation threat, and the counter is non-repudiation: individual identities, signed requests and tamper-evident logs that prove who did what. A longer shared key still cannot tell one merchant user from another, stronger TLS protects the channel rather than attribution, and a contract clause cannot manufacture proof the system never recorded.

ns-f2-03.why: Threat modelling starts by decomposing the system: a data flow diagram with its trust boundaries shows where data crosses between levels of trust, and each crossing is where threats are systematically found. Headline-driven lists miss threats specific to this design, a threat feed describes the outside world rather than the gateway, and production testing comes after design, when fixes cost the most.

ns-f2-04.why: An attack tree decomposes an attacker's goal into alternative paths, such as a spoofed supplier email, a compromised approver or a changed bank file, and annotating costs or difficulty shows which branches are cheapest and need controls first. A CVE list covers only technical flaws on servers, a policy stops no attacker, and a single worst case misses the cheaper paths real attackers take.

ns-f2-05.why: Segregation of duties splits a sensitive process so no one person can complete it alone; separating build, approval and deployment means fraud or error needs collusion to succeed. Trust is not a control. Yearly log review detects misuse long after the damage, and giving everyone full rights multiplies the same risk.

ns-f2-06.why: Split knowledge divides a secret so that no single person knows or holds all of it, with key components held by separate custodians and combined only under dual control. One person holding the whole key is a single point of failure and fraud. A single paper copy in a safe still gives one person the whole key, and email spreads it far beyond control.

ns-f2-07.why: A service level agreement sets measurable commitments, such as response times by priority, with remedies if they are missed; it is how security operations hold providers to what the business needs. Accepting the delay leaves incidents unanswered for days. Sharing the provider's admin password breaks accountability, and cancelling overnight leaves nobody ready to run the firewalls.

ns-f2-08.why: Job rotation and mandatory vacation bring a fresh person into a role, exposing ongoing fraud or errors the incumbent could otherwise hide. Never being caught is not evidence of no wrongdoing. A second clerk doing the same work gives no independent check, and a signed statement from the person being checked adds no assurance.

ns-f2-09.why: Travel security for high-risk destinations limits what can be lost or copied: a clean loaner holding only the data the trip needs, wiped and checked on return, protects both the traveller and Tessaly. An everyday laptop exposes all her access at a border search. A hotel safe is not secure against determined actors, and an extra laptop doubles the exposure.

ns-f2-10.why: Emergency exits must be fail-safe, unlocking on power loss so people can escape; life safety always outranks asset protection. Fail-secure doors that stay locked can trap people during a fire that cuts power. Keeping unsuitable doors ducks the question, and relying on one guard with a key makes everyone's escape depend on one person being present.

ns-f2-11.why: Gas suppression can displace oxygen or harm people, so life safety requires a pre-discharge alarm, time delay and abort switch to let occupants evacuate before release, plus training on what the alarm means. Sprinklers would damage the equipment the system protects, a low fire risk is no reason to accept a lethal hazard, and banning night work does not help people already inside.

ns-f2-12.why: Lone-worker safety needs a way to raise the alarm when someone cannot: regular check-ins, or a man-down device, that escalate automatically when missed. Telling people to be careful does not help after a fall. Reviewing CCTV in the morning finds an injury hours too late, and stopping all night work halts operations without addressing the risk.

ns-f2-13.why: Key risk indicators are forward-looking measures tied to risk appetite, and thresholds make them trigger action before losses occur. Trends in unpatched critical assets, overdue access reviews or privileged-account growth are typical. Closed-incident counts are lagging performance measures, a gut-feel rating is not data, and raw alert volume tracks tool noise more than risk.

ns-f2-14.why: DR and BC test data must show whether recovery met its objectives: measured recovery time and data loss against the RTO and RPO, and the problems found, so management can judge and improve the plan. Coming back eventually is not success if it took three days. A pass flag or screenshots record the outcome without the measures that matter.

ns-f2-15.why: Physical security works in layers: locked racks with logged key access control who reaches the hardware, and a console session that times out stops anyone walking up and using live admin rights. Relying on the room door alone ignores insiders and visitors. Removing the console hampers legitimate work, and a sign changes nothing on its own.

ns-f2-16.why: Visitor management verifies identity, records who is on site and when, marks visitors with badges and keeps them escorted in secure areas. That prevents an unescorted person near the network cabinet. Self sign-in is not a control, banning all visitors blocks necessary work such as audits, and a camera only records what the missing escort should have prevented.

ns-f2-17.why: A software bill of materials lists the components inside each product, so when a library flaw is announced Tessaly can find its exposure in minutes rather than weeks. Making it a contract requirement builds transparency into supply chain risk management. Banning open source is unrealistic, reverse-engineering every product is slow and may breach licences, and ad hoc emails depend on supplier goodwill.

ns-f2-18.why: An administrative (internal) investigation still needs proper authority, a defined scope and respect for privacy law and policy; checking HR and legal sign-off keeps the evidence usable and protects everyone involved. Pulling everything on request risks overreach. Refusing ignores Tessaly's legitimate right to investigate internally, and tipping off the subject can lead to lost evidence.

ns-f2-19.why: An unauthorised change is a change management failure and possibly a sign of compromise, so it is investigated as a potential incident: who made it, how, and why. Filing a retroactive ticket hides the question. Rolling back without looking destroys evidence and may miss the attacker's access, and a working gateway says nothing about whether it is secure.

ns-f2-20.why: In a managed service the provider secures its platform, but Tessaly still owns its access rights, secrets, pipeline configuration and data; mapping the shared-responsibility model assigns those controls. A SOC 2 report covers the vendor's controls and lists complementary user controls you must run; handing over secrets widens trust; a parallel system doubles the attack surface.

ns-f3-01.why: Secure provisioning applies need-to-know and least privilege to data: a restricted view gives exactly the fields the study needs, and a time limit removes access when it ends. Read-only still exposes every field, an export creates an unmanaged copy outside the database's controls, and refusing blocks legitimate fraud work.

ns-f3-02.why: When someone changes role, provisioning must revoke what the old role needed, or privileges accumulate. Remove the access, let the payroll owner judge whether the two opens were legitimate, and fix the mover process that missed it. Keeping it just in case is privilege creep, silent removal hides a process failure, and suspension presumes guilt.

ns-f3-03.why: Provisioning is a full lifecycle: each asset issued is recorded against the person, so deprovisioning can revoke every access and recover every item. The badge and token still open doors and accounts. Collecting only the laptop leaves them live, waiting leaves the badge working, and self-destruction gives no proof and no recovery.

ns-f3-04.why: Provisioning data to a third party needs agreed terms first: permitted use, security and handling requirements, retention and deletion, and audit rights, so obligations follow the data. Trust is not a control, access before terms gives up leverage, and a nightly export creates uncontrolled copies with even less oversight.

ns-f3-05.why: Removable media control lets only approved, encrypted devices be used, so data leaving the site stays protected and accountable, while giving staff a sanctioned way to work. Promises are not controls. Gluing ports blocks keyboards and legitimate devices too, and weekly deletion leaves customer data on lost or stolen sticks in the meantime.

ns-f3-06.why: Media marking shows the classification and handling rules for each item, so people store, transport and destroy it correctly. Treating unknown media as public invites exposure, and throwing it away unsanitised may leak data and destroy records. Leaving media unmarked relies on obscurity while ensuring your own staff mishandle it.

ns-f3-07.why: Backup media must be stored off-site, securely and far enough from the primary site that one disaster cannot destroy both the systems and their backups. A cupboard next to the servers shares their fate, the server room is even closer to it, and a second disk in the same server is lost with it.

ns-f3-08.why: Media management covers the full lifecycle: when retention expires, media should be securely destroyed with a verified method and a certificate, cutting the data exposed in any breach or legal demand. Keeping everything forever raises risk and discovery cost. Ordinary bins leak data, and reusing tapes past their service life risks failed backups.

ns-f3-09.why: A pre-action system keeps its pipes dry until a detector fires and needs a second trigger before water flows, so a damaged pipe or a single false alarm does not soak live equipment; clean agents avoid water entirely where hardware value justifies it. Wet pipe stays charged over the racks; detection without suppression lets fire spread; relying on staff with extinguishers puts people at risk.

ns-f3-10.why: Environmental controls keep humidity in a moderate band, roughly 40–60%: too dry and static discharge damages components, too humid and condensation corrodes them. Positive pressure pushes air outward when doors open, keeping dust and smoke out. Driving humidity down causes static; open windows bring in dust and break the perimeter; colder air does nothing for dryness.

ns-f3-11.why: Wiring closets are sensitive facility spaces: physical access to switches lets someone tap, reroute or disable traffic, payment data included. They need dedicated, access-controlled and logged space with engineered cooling, not a propped door. A request to cleaners is unenforced; a camera on an open door records the attack rather than stopping it; a desk drawer is no equipment room.

ns-f3-12.why: Useful monitoring captures the events that matter: process command lines and script-block logging show what an attacker actually ran, and forwarding them centrally keeps them safe and correlated. Blocking PowerShell outright breaks administration without improving visibility. Local-only logs can be wiped by the intruder, and quarterly review finds the attack months late.

ns-f3-13.why: A runbook documents the exact steps for a known alert type: triage checks, evidence to preserve, containment actions and when to escalate. It makes responses consistent and repeatable and prevents missed steps such as memory capture. Personal judgement produced the inconsistency, disabling the alert creates a blind spot, and a new SIEM does not tell analysts what to do.

ns-f3-14.why: The ISC2 Code asks you to provide diligent and competent service to principals, which means being honest about the limits of your expertise and making sure the work is still done well. Signing beyond your competence misleads the CFO and the regulator, marketing pages are not due diligence, and a flat refusal leaves your principal without the help the canon requires.

ns-f3-15.why: Hardware segmentation uses processor and memory hardware, such as MMU-enforced partitions or hardware-assisted virtualisation, to keep workloads' memory apart, so a compromised browser cannot reach payment memory. Separate user accounts are software separation that a kernel exploit crosses; clearing the cache is housekeeping; antivirus detects known threats but creates no isolation.

ns-f3-16.why: Threat intelligence is useful only when acted on: loading the indicators into detection tools catches new activity, and hunting through recent logs shows whether the campaign already reached Tessaly. Filing reports unread wastes them. Blocking every new domain breaks legitimate business, and asking all staff to watch for domains is not a reliable control.

ns-f3-17.why: Returning to the primary site starts with the least critical systems, proving the rebuilt site works before critical operations depend on it; the disaster is not over until everything is back and stable. Moving everything at once risks a second outage. Moving critical systems first exposes them to an unproven site, and staying at a recovery site built for short-term use is not a plan.

ns-role-endpoint.definition: You work the hosts: process trees, persistence keys, driver loads, tamper alerts. Malware that runs, hides, or digs in surfaces on your queue first — the wire and the boardroom are someone else's problem.

ns-role-grc.definition: You hold the paper line: control evidence, audit trails, notification duties, executive risk questions. Your nights fill with auditors and anxious leadership — and when an incident lands, you are the one who knows what must be reported, to whom, by when.

ns-role-identity.definition: You live in the authentication and authorization plane: sign-in telemetry, factor challenges, federation assertions, privilege changes. Nights on your watch tilt toward stolen credentials and quiet permission creep, because that is the traffic you can actually read.

ns-role-network.definition: You read flows, not files: segmentation maps, egress patterns, beacon intervals, protocol misuse. Your shift bends toward probes, pivots, and callbacks — the adversary moves you can see on the wire.
